Blessed  Leonard  when  he  had  paused  in  his  ser- 
mon, which  words  he  could  not  then  understand. 
He  and  all  assembled  were  persuaded  that  when  he 
spoke  and  stamped  with  his  feet,  the  devil  was  at 
work  cutting  the  ropes,  and  to  confound  him,  he 
obtained  the  miraculous  interposition  of  God.

In  January,  1742,  Blessed  Leonard  was  sent

CHAPTER  XIX. 

VARIOUS  CURES  WROUGHT  BY  BLESSED  LEONARD 
DURING  HIS  LIFE. 

Pietro  Bitti,  a  Roman,  had  a  thorn  in  one  of  his 
thumbs,  which  inflamed  his  hand,  and  finding  no 
doctor  to  extract  it,  he  went  to  Blessed  Leonard 
in  the  monastery  of  S.  Buonaventura,  and  asked 
him  to  prescribe  something.  The  holy  Father 
blessed  him  with  the  little  image  of  the  Madonna 
which  he  carried  about  with  him,  when  imme- 
diately his  hand  was  cured,  and  he  never  again 
suffered  from  the  same  cause. 

Rosa  Pecci,  of  Mantelica,  was  suffering  from  an 
internal  disorder,  and  feeling  a  great  repugnance 
to  be  examined  by  a  doctor,  went  to  make  her 
confession  to  Blessed  Leonard,  and  disclosed  to 
him  her  distress,  when  he  assured  her  that  there 


Digitized  by  Google 


BLESSED  LEONARD. 


would  be  no  necessity  even  to  describe  her  suffer- 
ings to  any  one.  And  so  it  happened,  for  in  a  few 
days  she  was  cured  of  the  malady  without  medi- 
cal aid,  and  was  ever  after  free  from  it.  In  the 
Island  of  Corsica,  it  happened  one  day  that  a 
girl  of  eighteen,  who  was  working  in  the  fields, 
fell  asleep  with  her  mouth  open;  a  serpent  crept  in  ; 
and  awaking  in  terror,  she  had  not  the  presence  of 
mind  to  pull  it  out ;  it  conseqently  entered  her  sto- 
mach, and  there  remained  for  some  months,  causing 
her  the  greatest  pain  and  torture;  she  was  always 
obliged  to  carry  a  piece  of  bread  with  her,  and  be 
constantly  eating,  to  feed  the  serpent ;  she  suffered 
dreadfully  night  and  day,  without  being  able  to 
sleep,  and  very  soon  was  reduced  to  a  mere  shadow, 
and  excited  the  compassion  of  all  who  beheld  her.

When  he  was  giving  a  mission  in  Orezza,  also

CHAPTER  XX. 

ON  THE  VARIOUS  CURES  EFFECTED  THROUGH  THE  MERITS 
OF  BLESSED  LEONARD  IN  ANSWER  TO  THOSE  WHO 
INVOKED  HIS  ASSISTANCE. 

The  virtues  and  gifts  with  which  Blessed  Leo- 
nard was  endowed  caused  him  to  be  held  in  such 
high  esteem  and  veneration  by  the  people,  that 
they  called  him  the  Apostolic  man,  the  Apostle  of 
our  times,  a  man  filled  with  the  Holy  Spirit,  and 
the  holy  Father.  This  veneration  was  found  not 
only  in  the  common  and  simple  people,  but  also 
in  most  learned  ecclesiastics  and  people  in  the 


Digitized  by  Google 


BLESSED  LEONARD. 


335 


highest  grade,  as  well  as  in  most  eminent  cardinals, 
and  many  bishops,  whose  dioceses  he  enlightened 
by  his  missions.  This  great  esteem  caused  many  to 
come  to  the  convent  of  S.  Buonaventura,  to  touch 
his  body  as  soon  as  they  heard  of  his  death,  and 
to  obtain  some  relic  of  him.  Many  also  gave 
him  the  title  of  Saint,  and  very  soon  after  his 
death  images  were  made  of  him,  which,  with  the 
things  he  had  worn  or  used,  were  in  great  request, 
even  in  remote  parts  of  the  country,  and  were  pre- 
served with  singular  devotion.  As  a  proof  of  the 
veneration  in  which  he  was  held  in  Rome,  his 
funeral  was  conducted  with  the  greatest  solemnity 
in  the  church  of  the  Rotunda,  and  a  secular  priest 
pronounced  the  funeral  oration,  which  was  after- 
wards published.  It  began  thus  :  "  The  apostolic 
man  was  held  in  the  highest  veneration  by  men, 
because  he  was  believed  to  be  a  man  of  God,  and 
filled  with  the  Holy  Spirit/ 9  &c.  The  Genoese 
also  desired  to  give  testimony  of  their  veneration 
for  our  holy  Father,  and  published,  as  soon  as 
his  death  was  announced,  a  print  dedicated  to  the 
Pope,  which  was  composed  of  a  shield,  with  a  ship 
representing  the  Church,  which  destroys  all  here- 
sies, and  within  it  the  three  theological  virtues, 
with  a  corresponding  inscription  in  praise  of  this 
great  man.  Almighty  God  confirmed  the  uni- 
versal veneration  for  His  servant  by  working 
many  miracles  after  his  death,  in  restoring  to 
health  those  who  had  recourse  to  his  intercession, 
some  of  which  we  shall  relate.  Maddelena  of

place  him  on  the  tomb  of  the  blessed  servant  of 
God.  On  entering  the  church  she  found  it  so 
crowded  that  it  was  with  the  greatest  difficulty 
she  could  approach  the  screen  of  the  chancel,  be- 
fore the  high  altar,  where  the  tomb  of  Blessed 
Leonard  was ;  but  she  took  courage,  and  putting 
her  child  through  the  grate,  entreated  a  man  who 
stood  within  to  place  him  on  the  tomb,  as  she 
was  unable  to  do  so  herself,  in  consequence  of  the 
crowd.  The  man  complied  with  her  request,  and 
the  child  had  scarcely  been  there  while  you  could 
say  a  Pater  noster,  when  he  was  seen  to  smile, 
and  appear  quite  joyous,  and  very  soon  he  was 
brought  back  to  his  mother  perfectly  well,  not  a 
sore  was  to  be  seen  in  any  part  of  his  body,  and  his 
head,  which  had  been  so  disfigured,  was  covered 
with  hair.

CHAPTER  XXI. 

OTHER  MIRACULOUS  CURES  WROUGHT  BY  BLESSED 
LEONARD  AFTER  HIS  DEATH, 

Maria  Maddaiena  Pallari,  of  Pergola,  whilst 
she  was  in  Rome  suffered  for  some  time  from  a 
swelling  in  her  leg,  which  made  her  very  lame, 
and  she  was  not  able  to  walk  without  the  greatest 
pain  and  inconvenience.  After  suffering  in  this 
manner  for  eight  years,  she  went  to  the  tomb  of 
Blessed  Leonard,  and  when  she  was  praying  there 
the  swelling  suddenly  abated,  the  pain  ceased, 
she  recovered  the  use  of  her  leg,  and  returned 
home  quite  well. 

In  Torn,  in  the  Abbacy  of  San  Salvatore  Mag- 
giore,  the  wife  of  Antonio  Lepori  was  afflicted 
with  a  severe  illness,  and  it  was  thought  she 
must  soon  die.  After  having  applied  every  reme- 
dy without  avail,  she  was  induced  to  wear  a  piece 
of  the  habit  of  Blessed  Leonard,  when  she  was  in-

stantly  freed  from  pain.  A  short  time  after,  she 
mislaid  the  relic,  and  the  pains  returned ;  but  find* 
ing  it  again  she  applied  it  a  second  time,  and 
instantly  she  was  freed  from  pain  as  before. 
After  this  experience  she  always  wore  it,  and  re- 
mained perfectly  well  as  long  as  she  lived. 

Giuseppe  Kaffi,  of  Fara,  a  tailor  by  trade,  in 
striking  a  dog  with  a  tool  hurt  his  hand  severely; 
the  wound  became  black,  and  turned  to  a  gan- 
grene ;  mortification  ensued,  and  the  doctors  de- 
cided that  the  hand  must  be  amputated.  In 
great  fear  and  trouble  Giuseppe  had  recourse  to 
the  aid  of  Blessed  Leonard,  and  had  so  much 
faith  in  his  intercession,  that  he  was  induced  to 
touch  his  hand  with  a  piece  of  his  habit,  and  in- 
stantly he  was  cured. 

Sister  Chiara  Francesea  Tuani,  a  nun  in  the 
convent  of  S.  Chiara  in  Sarzana,  where  she  had 
been  educated,  suffered  much  from  an  abscess  in 
her  left  foot ;  the  sore  had  festered,  and  although 
it  had  been  lanced  and  burnt  with  caustic,  it 
did  not  heal,  and  she  was  unable  to  walk.  The 
abbess,  seeing  the  evil  increase,  so  that  the  bone  of 
her  foot  was  visible,  deemed  it  necessary  to  try 
some  other  remedy,  but  nothing  they  did  was  of 
any  avail,  and  at  length  they  had  recourse  to  the 
intercession  of  Blessed  Leonard,  and  at  the  same 
time  applied  to  the  sore  n  piece  of  his  handker- 
chief; Having  done  this  she  slept  quietly  that 
night,  which  she  had  not  done  for  some  time,  and 
in  the  morning  the  sore  was  perfectly  healed.

short  for  four  months,  she  was  never  free  from 
pain,  and  was  reduced  to  a  perfect  skeleton.  One 
day  a  monk  came  to  her  house,  who  gave  her  a 
piece  of  Blessed  Leonard's  habit,  and  a  morsel 
of  the  bread  left  by  him  at  table  ;  she  ate  a  little 
of  the  bread,  and  hung  the  piece  of  cloth  round 
her  neck,  when  she  instantly  felt  a  shock  in  her 
system,  and  from  that  moment  recovered  her 
health,  and  was  free  from  pain  as  long  as  she 
lived. 

In  the  town  of  Aquila,  a  little  girl  three  years 
old,  niece  of  the  priest,  and  also  of  Don  Venanzio 
de  Bernardis,  was  seized  with  fever,  and  on  the 
fifth  day  she  was  reduced  to  the  last  extreme  ;  her 
parent  and  uncle  wept,  thinking  her  dead.  Whilst 
the  child  remained  in  this  state,  silent  and  im- 
moveable, her  uncle  implored  the  assistance  of 
Blessed  Leonard,  promising  that  if  he  heard  his 
prayer,  he  would  make  a  public  attestation  of  the 
cure.  He  therefore  took  a  relic  of  the  man  of  God, 
which  he  had  in  the  house,  said  three  Paters  and 
three  Aves,  made  the  sign  of  the  cross  over  the 
dying  child,  who  the  same  moment  opened  her 
eyes,  spoke  distinctly,  and  asked  for  something  to 
eat ;  she  then  rose  up  and  walked  across  the  room, 
to  the  astonishment  of  all  present ;  her  uncle  felt 
her  pulse,  and  found  her  quite  free  from  fever  and 
perfectly  well,  and  she  continued  so,  as  Don  Ve- 
nanzio afterwards  attested  juridically.

THE  LIFE 

OF 

BLESSED  NICHOLAS  FATTORE, 

OF  THE  ORDER  OF  THE  OBSERVANTINE  MINOR  FRIARS 
OF  SAINT  FRANCIS. 

BOOK  I. 

CHAPTER  I. 

OF.  THE  BIRTH  AND  CHILDHOOD  OF  BLESSED  NICHOLAS. 

The  citv  of  Valencia,  the  capital  of  one  of  the 
provinces  of  Spain,  has  ever  been  remarkable  for 
the  salubrity  of  its  position,  the  number  and 
riches  of  its  population,  the  wonderful  fertility 
of  its  soil,  the  majestic  appearance  of  its  build- 
ings, and  still  more  for  the  honourable  manner 
in  which  its  inhabitants  have  distinguished  them- 
selves in  the  army,  in  diplomacy,  and  in  science  ; 
and  for  the  number  who,  having  excelled  in  the 
perfection  of  evangelical  sanctity,  have  been  glori- 
fied by  God.    Valencia  was  the  birth-place  of 
Blessed  Nicholas  Fattore ;  a  sketch  of  whose 
life  we  are  about  to  give,  for  the  glory  of  God  and 
the  edification  of  His  elect. 

Vincenzo  Fattore,  born  at  Syracuse  in  Sicily, 


Digitized  by  Google 


362 


NICIIOLAS  FA.TTOKE. 


repaired  in  his  youth  to  Valencia,  and  there  set- 
tled. Being  in  easy  circumstances  and  a  good 
Christian,  he  wooed  and  won  for  his  bride  Ursula 
Stagna,  a  native  of  Albaida,  a  young  lady  of 
extreme  modesty  and  of  exemplary  piety.  Four 
sons  and  three  daughters  were  the  fruit  of  this 
marriage.  Blessed  Nicholas  was  the  second,  and 
was  born  on  the  festival  of  the  Prince  of  the 
Apostles,  June  29th,  in  the  year  1520.  A  mi- 
raculous favour  obtained  by  his  father  through 
the  intercession  of  S.  Nicholas,  together  with  the 
circumstances  of  the  child  having  been  born  on 
the  day  consecrated  to  S.  Peter,  induced  him  to 
give  the  double  name  Pietro  Niccolo  to  this  his 
second-born  child.  Out  of  devotion  to  S.  Vincent 
Ferrer  he  was  baptised  in  the  same  holy  font 
where,  two  centuries  before,  S.  Vincent  had  him- 
self been  baptised  in  the  church  of  S.  Stephen 
the  first  martyr.  These  worthy  parents,  both  by 
word  and  example,  gave  their  children  such  a  Chris- 
tian education  as  became  them,  and  had  the  satis- 
faction of  witnessing  its  salutary  effects  in  all  of 
them.  From  his  earliest  infancy  they  were  con- 
vinced that  Pietro  Niccolo  was  prevented  by  God 
with  most  special  benediction.  They,  and  others 
who  knew  him  when  he  was  about  four  or  five 
years  old,  declared  that  they  never  saw  anything 
puerile  in  his  conduct ;  whereas,  even  then,  they 
saw  many  indications  of  perfection  in  him.  Be- 
fore he  reached  the  age  of  five,  he  began  to  fast 
three  days  in  the  week,  Monday,  Wednesday,  and 
Saturday  ;  his  fast  on  Saturday  was  so  rigorous, 
that  he  never  would  allow  himself  so  much  as  a

drop  of  water  before  his  dinner  hour.  When  he 
was  five  years  old  he  went  to  a  public  school, 
which  gave  him  the  opportunity  of  increasing 
and  concealing  his  fasts.  His  little  collation, 
which,  like  the  other  children,  he  used  to  carry 
with  him  to  school,  he  distributed,  either  partially 
or  entirely,  amongst  the  poor  whom  he  happened 
to  meet  on  the  road.  Whilst  yet  a  mere  child,  as 
he  was  going  through  the  public  street  on  his  way 
to  school,  in  company  with  others  of  his  own 
age,  he  met  a  beggar  covered  with  sores ;  Nicho- 
las knelt  down  at  the  beggar's  feet,  kissed  them 
and  his  hands  very  devoutly,  and  then  besought 
the  poor  man  to  give  him  his  blessing.  The  other 
children  laughed  at  him,  but  an  elderly  person, 
who  had  witnessed  the  scene  with  astonishment, 
reproved  the  scoffers,  highly  commended  the  pious 
act  of  Nicholas,  and  predicted  that  the  child 
would  one  day  be  a  great  servant  of  the  Lord. 

When  he  was  ten  years  old,  he  once  saw  a  poor 
woman  covered  with  a  hideous  leprosy  from  head 
to  foot,  standing  at  the  door  of  the  hospital  of  S. 
Lazarus ;  prostrating  himself,  he  tenderly  kissed 
her  feet  and  hands,  and  begged  her  blessing. 
One  of  his  companions  asked  him  how  he  could 
kiss  those  feet  and  hands,  covered  as  they  were 
with  most  loathsome  filth ;  the  blessed  child  an- 
swered, "I  did  not  kiss  the  repulsive  filth  of 
that  poor  woman,  but  the  sweet  wounds  of  Jesus 
Christ"  In  a  child  of  ten  years  old,  such  a  lively 
and  active  faith  is  a  true  and  inoontestible  proof 
that  the  Divine  Spirit  had,  even  at  that  early 
age,  taken  full  possession  of  the  boy's  soul,  and

dwelt  therein  with  special  complacency,  affection- 
ately working  there,  and  enriching  it  with  hea- 
venly gifts  and  graces.  Guided  by  that  celestial 
wisdom,  he  began  when  but  a  child,  and  ever 
after  continued  to  visit  the  hospitals,  serving  and 
consoling  the  sick  with  incredible  tenderness  and 
charity  ;  and  he  often  exhorted  his  companions  to 
this  practice,  occasionally  taking  some  of  them 
with  him.  He  used  to  remind  them  that  it  was 
Jesus  Himself  whom  they  visited  in  the  persons  of 
the  sick  in  the  hospitals,  and  that  our  Divine 
Redeemer  looks  upon  every  act  of  charity  done 
for  His  sake  to  the  sick  poor  as  done  to  Himself. 
It  is  worthy  of  remark,  too,  that  in  those  days, 
visiting  the  hospital  for  the  love  of  Jesus  Christ 
was  a  work  of  Christian  charity  practised  but  by 
few,  so  that  it  required  that  they  who  did  it 
should  possess  a  more  than  ordinary  share  of  divine 
charity. 

One  morning,  a  school-fellow,  in  childish  giddi- 
ness, accused  him  to  the  master  of  negligence  in 
his  studies,  for  which  he  received  a  couple  of 
slight  lashes  ;  soon  afterwards  the  master  quitted 
the  class,  when  Blessed  Nicholas,  in  presence  of 
all  his  companions,  knelt  down,  begged  his  ac- 
cuser's pardon  for  the  scandal  given  by  his  neg- 
lect, and  with  humble  sincerity  thanked  him  for 
the  charity  with  which  he  had  sought  his  amend- 
ment. When  the  wise  master  was  informed  of 
this,  he  conceived  the  highest  opinion  of  the 
striking  virtue  displayed  by  such  a  child ;  prog- 
nosticating the  perfection  to  which  he  would  at- 
tain when  of  mature  age.    The  life  which  holed

at  home  rendered  him  amiable  to  every  one  ;  he 
was  strictly  obedient  and  affectionately  respectful 
to  all ;  remarkable  for  his  love  of  retirement,  when 
he  was  ever  occupied,  either  in  study  or  prayer, 
or  in  conversing  with  feeling  simplicity  on  spiri- 
tual subjects  with  the  members  of  his  family, 
every  one  called  him  a  holy,  innocent  child.  One 
fact,  tolerably  significant  of  the  effects  of  his 
exemplary  conduct,  was  declared  in  the  processes. 
His  father  had  a  Moorish  female  slave,  most  ob- 
stinately attached  to  mahomedanism ;  this  wo- 
man was  at  length  so  struck  by  the  charity  of 
Nicholas,  then  a  child,  and  by  his  unwavering 
and  engaging  sanctity,  which  shone  forth  in  all 
his  actions,  that  she  felt  convinced  such  a  child 
could  only  be  guided  by  the  one  Supreme  God, 
and  that  his  religion  alone  could  be  true  and  di- 
vine ;  yielding  to  this  conviction,  she  embraced 
the  faith  of  Jesus  Christ,  and  was  baptised. 

If,  either  at  home  or  abroad,  he  saw  anything 
that  could  offend  our  Lord,  he  courageously,  yet 
kindly,  admonished  and  scolded  his  equals  and  in- 
feriors ;  whilst  towards  his  superiors  he  used  pru- 
dence and  respect,  humbly  begging  them  to  re- 
member that  God  ought  to  be  honoured  and  rever- 
enced by  every  one,  and  that  whoever  offended 
Him  drew  down  divine  chastisements  on  them- 
selves ;  he  always  corrected  those  who  dared  to 
take  the  holy  name  of  God  in  vain,  or  the  names 
of  Mary  and  the  Saints,  an  abuse  which  was  very 
common  in  those  days.  As  years  rolled  on,  so 
did  Blessed  Nicholas  advance  in  virtue  and  perfec- 
tion ;  without  slackening  for  a  single  day,  he  per-

severed  in  the  above-described  virtuous  career 
till  the  seventeenth  year  of  his  age ;  to  this  we 
may  add  that  at  the  proper  time  he  was  admitted 
to  the  holy  sacraments  of  confession  and  com-

seculars  then  did  but  rarely.  He  constantly  at- 
tended the  church  services,  especially  on  festivals, 
assisting  at  all  the  divine  offices,  and  at  sermons ; 
he  studied  indefatigably,  and  made  great  pro- 
gress. At  the  age  of  seventeen  he  wrote  ex- 
tremely well,  was  well  versed  in  his  own  and  in  the 
Latin  languages,  in  both  of  which  he  composed 
well  both  in  prose  and  verse  ;  he  had  acquired  the 
principles  of  music,  played  on  the  cymbal,  sung 
with  taste  and  skill,  and  could  paint  well. 


CHAPTER  II. 

HE  ENTERS  THE  ORDER  OP  THE  MINOR  FRIARS. 

Almighty  God  already  called  His  servant  to 
solitude,  where  he  might  be  wholly  free  from 
the  disturbances  of  worldly  affairs  as  far  as  it 
was  possible;  and  the  pious  youth's  sole  study 
was  to  ascertain  the  Divine  will  with  regard  to 
what  order  he  was  to  make  choice  of.  By  prayer 
and  fasting  he  besought  the  Almighty  to  guide 
him  in  an  affair  of  such  high  importance.  His 
father's  ideas,  however,  were  widely  different  from 
his  own ;  rejoicing  immeasurably  in  the  exem- 
plary conduct  of  Nicholas,  he  was  most  anx- 
ious to  have  him  suitably  settled  in  the  world. 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


367 


He  had  a  private  interview  with  him,  when  he 
told  him  that  he  had  a  competent  sum  of  money 
which  he  intended  to  give  him,  in  order  that  he 
might  enter  into  partnership  with  some  merchant, 
and  devote  himself  to  commerce  ;  that  he  might, 
moreover,  look  out  for  a  wife  to  be  his  companion 
and  comfort,  and  that  the  emoluments  of  the 
mercantile  profession  would  enable  him  to  provide 
for  the  children  which  the  Lord  would  give  him 
in  due  time,  to  be  brought  up  in  the  divine  ser- 
vice, as  he  himself  had  done  with  regard  to 
Nicholas  and  his  brothers  and  sisters.  With  great 
respect  and  lively  gratitude  Nicholas  thanked 
his  affectionate  father  for  his  obliging  offers,  but 
frankly  and  firmly  told  him  that  he  could  not 
accept  them,  being  already  espoused  to  the  one 
Supreme  Good,  to  whom  he  had  entirely  conse- 
crated himself,  and  that  he  could  follow  no  other 
commerce  than  that  of  Paradise.  It  is  probable 
that  this  answer  was  not  altogether  unexpected  by 
his  father  ;  still,  though  Christian  piety  was  dear 
to  him,  the  dread  of  losing  so  excellent  a  son  was 
no  small  cross  to  him. 

In  the  mean  time,  Nicholas  prayed  more 
fervently  than  ever  that  our  Lord  would  be 
pleased  to  conduct  him  to  the  house  for  which 
he  was  destined,  and  to  which  he  had  been  called 
for  some  time  past.  After  class  hours,  he  used 
frequently  to  repair  to  the  monastery  of  Minor- 
Friars,  called  "  S.  Maria  di  Gesu,"  distant  some- 
what less  than  a  mile  from  the  city  of  Valencia. 
After  spending  some  time  in  prayer  in  the  church, 
he  conversed  with  such  of  the  religious  as  he

368 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


happened  to  be  acquainted  with.  Towards  the 
end  of  November,  1537,  repairing  as  usual  to 
the  above-named  monastery,  our  Lord  gave  him 
clearly  to  understand  that  this  was  the  house  for 
which  He  had  destined  him.  After  recommending 
himself  anew  to  God  with  redoubled  fervour, 
he  presented  himself  to  the  father-guardian,  and 
throwing  himself  on  his  knees,  he  with  deep 
humility  and  many  tears  besought  him  in  cha- 
rity to  admit  him  amongst  the  sons  of  S.  Fran- 
cis. The  prudent  superior  admired  the  fervour 
and  humility  of  the  supplicating  youth ;  and  in 
his  heart  he  blessed,  and  thanked  the  Lord  for 
sending  him  so  fervent  a  novice ;  however,  he 
judged  that  time  and  trial  ought  to  prove  his 
vocation:  he  bade  him  rise,  extolled  his  design, 
with  which  he  expressed  himself  much  pleased, 
but  gave  him  to  understand  the  propriety  of 
examining  whether  his  fervent  desires  proceeded 
from  the  spirit  of  God.  He  represented  to  him  in 
terms  the  most  distasteful  to  human  nature,  the 
extreme  poverty  of  the  seraphical  order,  the  ex- 
cessive and  oppressive  toils  of  the  religious,  the 
number  and  the  rigour  of  their  fasts,  and  in  fine, 
the  whole  austerity  of  the  rule  of  S.  Francis.  He 
reminded  him  of  his  duty  as  a  son,  and  of  the 
grief  he  would  occasion  to  his  family,  if  he  left 
home  without  their  knowledge  and  consent.  In 
a  word,  he  said  all  he  possibly  could  to  induce 
him  to  reflect  on  so  many  important  points.  But 
divine  charity,  when  sincere,  so  far  from  being  ex- 
tinguished by  many  waters,  becomes  more  vigour- 
ous,  and  its  blessed  flames  are  more  expanded

thereby.  The  youthful  Nicholas,  kneeling  and 
weeping,  pleaded  his  own  cause  so  well,  that  the 
father-guardian,  persuaded  and  convinced  of  the 
sincerity  of  his  vocation,  felt  in  a  manner  obliged 
to  allow  him  to  remain  in  the  convent.  When 
informed  of  the  circumstances,  as  he  soon  was, 
his  father  fainted  through  grief,  whilst  his  mother 
and  the  rest  of  the  family  were  inconsolable : 
but  the  beautifully  pious  letter  which  he  imme- 
diately wrote  to  his  affectionate  father,  and  the 
conversation  which  he  afterwards  had  with  him 
at  the  convent  of  "S.  Maria  di  Gesu,"  sub- 
dued the  affliction  of  his  family,  and  gave  gen- 
eral comfort.  He  spoke  to  his  father  with  such 
unction  and  eloquence,  as  to  make  him  sensible 
of  the  great  favour  God  conferred  on  him  by 
choosing  one  of  his  sons  to  be  the  servant  and 
minister  of  the  crucified  Redeemer ;  so  that  after 
a  time  his  father  and  mother  became  contented 
and  joyful,  thanking  the  Lord  for  honouring  them 
so  far  as  to  call  a  child  of  tbeir's, — one  so  loved 
and  so  holy — to  the  seraphic  order.  On  the  fes- 
tival of  S.  Andrew  the  apostle  in  the  aforesaid 
year  1537,  he  put  on  the  habit  of  S.  Francis  in 
the  convent  of  "  S;  Maria  di  Gesu"  of  Valencia. 
It  may  be  remarked  that  Blessed  Nicholas  was 
born  to  this  world  on  the  festival  of  S.  Peter,  and 
was  born  in  religion  on  the  festival  of  S.  Andrew. 
Now  as  these  two  most  holy  brothers  were  ena- 
moured of  the  cross  of  Jesus  Christ,  and  both  died 
on  the  cross,  it  may  piously  be  believed  that  our 
Lord  would  by  this  coincidence  pre-announce  that 
Blessed  Nicholas  would  be  distinguished  by  his 
to

great  love  of  the  cross,  in  the  same  way  as  this 
love  had  been  the  distinctive  characteristic  of  the 
two  brother-apostles,  of  whom  Andrew  was  the 
first  called  to  the  apostolate  by  Jesus  Christ, 
whilst  Peter  was  by  Him  constituted  the  first  and 
chief  of  the  apostles. 

Evangelical  humility,  the  foundation  of  all  vir- 
tues, is  peculiarly  the  virtue  of  the  religious  of  S. 
Francis.  At  the  age  of  seventeen,  when  Nicholas 
put  on  the  habit  of  that  order,  he  was  tall,  well- 
proportioned,  healthy,  and  handsome  in  every 
way  ;  of  excellent  understanding,  and,  for  his  age, 
unusually  learned ;  he  played  on  various  instru- 
ments,  and  sung  well.  All  these  natural  endow- 
ments perhaps  made  his  directors  fear  that  he 
was  ill  suited  to  the  perfect  humility  peculiar  to 
the  order,  and  that  he  would  consequently  need 
much  practical  instruction,  but  they  soon  found 
out  their  mistake,  and  laid  aside  their  suspicions ; 
his  wonderful  meekness  and  humility  of  heart 
were  evident  to  every  one,  and  were  looked  upon 
as  his  natural  disposition.  After  the  death  of 
Blessed  Nicholas,  all  the  religious,  who  were  juridi- 
cally examined  in  the  processes,  unanimously  de- 
clared that  they  had  never  perceived  a  failing 
in  him,  nor  had  ever  heard  any  one  else  say 
that  they  had  done  so ;  that  in  his  whole  conduct 
they  ever  found  him  humble,  most  obedient,  an 
exact  observer  of  every  rule,  most  affable  to  all, 
ever  devout  in  the  recital  of  office,  and  much  given 
to  prolonged  prayer.  Whoever  knows  how  much 
of  high  perfection  is  required  by  the  rule  of  S. 
Francis,  will  understand  from  the  little  already

said,  that  Nicholas,  even  in  his  noviciate,  must 
have  been  a  youth  of  no  common  stamp  of  good- 
ness. He  had  two  .masters  during  this  time, 
both  of  whom  expressed  themselves  not  only  satis- 
fied, but  even  astonished  at  his  fervour  ;  their 
chief  care  was  to  put  a  curb  upon  him  with  regard 
to  labour,  fasting,  and  corporal  austerity. 

Having  completed  the  years  of  his  noviciate,  he 
besought  the  religious  assembled  in  chapter  to 
admit  him  to  profession,  protesting  with  sincere  hu- 
mility and  many  tears,  that  he  was  wholly  unwor- 
thy of  such  a  favour,  and  that  he  could  only 
expect  and  hope  for  it  from  the  heroic  charity  of 
the  religious,  who  were  much  affected,  and  highly 
admired  the  profound  humility  of  their  supplicant. 
He  made  his  solemn  profession  with  great  fervour 
on  the  first  Sunday  of  Advent,  in  the  year  1538, 
in  the  said  convent  of  S.  Maria  di  Gesii ;  from 
whence  he  passed  to  the  convent  of  the  Madonna 
del  Pino,  in  the  town  of  Oliva,  where  he  studied 
philosophy  and  theology.  The  life  of  the  student 
did  not  in  the  least  cool  the  fervour  of  our  saint, 
he  went  through  these  two  courses  with  great 
credit,  though  his  progress  in  virtue  was  still 
more  marked.  He  was  the  implacable  enemy  of 
idleness,  devoting  himself  most  assiduously  to 
study,  and  employing  every  moment  of  spare 
time  in  some  useful  occupation  ;  his  favourite 
diversion,  even  when  a  student,  consisted  in  con- 
versing with  one  or  other  of  the  elderly  and  most 
holy  of  the  fathers,  asking  counsel  for  his  own 
better  progress  in  the  ways  of  the  Lord,  or  else 
in  discoursing  on  pious  subjects  with  one  of  the

one  acknowledged  that  the  greatest  recreations 
and  amusements  of  the  world  could  not  be  com- 
pared with  the  pleasure  to  be  experienced  in  the 
cheerful  engaging  discourses  of  Blessed  Nicholas 
on  spiritual  subjects.  At  the  age  appointed  by 
the  canons,  his  superiors  sent  him  to  Valencia  to 
receive  holy  orders.  His  ordiuation  being  ac- 
complished, he  returned  to  the  Madonna  del  Pino, 
where  he  sung  his  first  mass  with  extraordinary 
fervour,  and  afterwards  completed  the  course  of 
his  studies. 


CHAPTER  III. 

HE  IS  APPOINTED  TO  THE  OFFICE  OF  PREACHER. 

The  obedience  of  Blessed  Nicholas  was  ever 
most  perfect  and  heroic  ;  abandoning  himself  un- 
reservedly  into  the  hands  of  his  superiors,  his  only 
thought  was  to  obey  their  commands  implicitly. 
Superiors  seeing  him  well  qualified  by  virtue  and 
learning,  and  by  a  complication  of  natural  and 
divine  gifts,  for  every  department  of  the  sacred 
ministry,  decided  on  applying  him  to  the  func- 
tion of  preaching  the  word  of  God,  and  accord- 
ingly appointed  him  preacher  to  the  monastery  of 
S.  Francis  di  Chelva,  with  commission  to  preach 
on  all  festivals  and  other  days  of  particular  devo- 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


373 


tion.  He  devoted  himself  to  this  duty  with  cheer- 
ful ardour,  and  from  the  very  first  gave  universal 
satisfaction ;  his  sermons  proving  most  beneficial 
to  his  hearers.  Preaching  so  often  was  a  great 
fatigue  to  him,  especially  in  the  beginning ;  but 
his  zeal  overcame  all,  and  he  often  repaired  to 
the  surrounding  villages  and  hamlets  to  announce 
the  word  of  the  Lord,  whereby  many  sinners  were 
brought  back  to  an  exemplary  course  of  life. 
Studying  for  his  sermons  did  not  hinder,  on  the 
contrary  it  rather  seconded  his  application  for 
prayer,  sa  that  it  may  with  truth  be  said,  that 
his  preaching  was  the  fruit  of  his  assiduous 
prayer. 

Adjoining  the  convent  of  Chelva  is  a  wood, 
with  several  small  chapels,  like  hermitages,  in  dif- 
ferent parts  of  it.  When  Nicholas  had  complied 
with  all  his  choir  duties,  and  other  regular  observ- 
ances, if  he  had  any  spare  time,  he  would  go  to 
one  of  these  hermitages,  and  there  abandon  him- 
self to  prayer.  He  often  took  one  of  the  novices 
with  him,  and  after  enjoining  strict  secrecy,  he 
would  order  him  to  strike  him  severely  with  a  rod 
on  his  bare  back,  even  till  the  flesh  was  all  bruised 
and  torn.  No  wonder  that  his  sermons,  the  fruit 
of  such  fervent  prayer  and  generous  mortification, 
should  produce  great  results,  and  be  looked  upon 
as  excellent  and  perfect.  Some  of  the  religious 
visited  his  poor  cell,  purposely  to  examine  the 
books  from  whence  he  drew  his  lights,  as  well  as 
the  remarkable  form  of  his  sermons ;  but  they 
found  nothing  there  but  the  Scriptures  and  his 
breviary.   They  used  to  watch  at  the  door  of  his

cell,  when  he  retired  to  it  in  order  to  prepare  for 
preaching ;  and  were  exceedingly  moved  as  they 
beheld  him  prostrate  before  a  crucifix,  where 
he  remained  for  a  long  time  absorbed  in  prayer ; 
he,  however,  interrupted  his  prayer  three  several 
times  to  give  himself  a  severe  discipline,  and 
was  often  heard  to  say  with  fervent  confidence : 
"Speak,  Lord,  for  thy  servant  hearetb!"  After 
thus  making  his  prayer,  which,  when  he  had  the 
time,  was  extended  to  several  hours,  he  entered 
the  pulpit.  One  of  his  religious  brethren,  a  man 
of  great  piety  and  goodness,  after  hearing  him 
preach  a  most  admirable  sermon  on  the  sublime 
mystery  of  the  Blessed  Trinity,  asked  him  in  aston- 
ishment how  it  was  that  he  had  been  able  to  dis- 
course with  such  accuracy  and  learning  on  so 
abstruse  a  subject,  and  having  had  so  short  a  time 
for  preparation.  With  a  sweet  and  humble  smile 
Blessed  Nicholas  answered  :  "Ah,  dear  father,  all 
things  are  soon  learned  at  the  foot  of  the  cru- 
cifix." 

The  fruit  of  his  preaching  corresponded  with 
the  divine  teaching  by  which  he  was  influenced. 
The  word  of  God  in  the  mouths  of  some  of  his 
servants  is  compared  to  an  impetuous  wind,  which 
uproots  and  shivers  the  noble  cedars  of  Libanus ; 
whilst  in  the  mouths  of  others  it  is  like  the  mild 
and  soothing  zephyr,  which,  by  degrees,  dissolves 
the  keenest  frost;  or  like  a  gentle  rain,  which 
fertilizes  the  parched  soil.  Blessed  Nicholas's 
mode  of  preaching  might  be  likened  to  the  latter. 
We  do  not  read  of  any  astounding  conversions 
effected  by  him ;  but  it  is  known  for  certain  that

he  continued  preaching  to  the  end  of  his  life 
in  the  two  provinces  of  Valencia  and  Catalonia ; 
everywhere  he  was  followed  by  crowds,  and  every- 
where he  induced  many  people  to  enter  upon  a 
christian  and  edifying  course  of  life.  Some  idea 
will  be  formed  of  the  concourse  of  persons  attend- 
ing his  sermons,  when  we  say  that  it  was  juridi- 
cally attested  in  the  processes,  that  even  in  large 
churches,  on  descending  from  the  pulpit,  so  great 
was  the  crowd,  that  men  were  obliged  to  raise  him 
on  their  shoulders,  and  carry  him  out,  in  order  to 
save  him  from  being  suffocated ;  again,  he  was 
often  obliged  to  preach  in  the  open  air,  to  satisfy 
the  multitudes,  when  the  windows  and  roofs  of 
the  houses  were  thronged  with  eager  listeners. 

The  efficacy  of  his  preaching  will  be  best  under- 
stood by  a  few  brief  facts,  selected  from  amongst 
many  in  the  processes.  When  at  Barcelona,  he 
was  invited  to  make  an  exhortation  to  that  illus- 
trious university,  where,  in  solemn  assembly, 
degrees  were  to  be  given  to  some  of  the  members 
who  had  successfully  completed  their  scientific 
and  literary  courses.  On  this  occasion  Blessed 
Nicholas  might  not  inaptly  be  compared  to  S.  Paul, 
when  introduced  to  preach  in  the  Areopagus  at 
Athens.  I  question  whether  he  could  have  had  a 
more  reverend  or  a  more  splendid  audience  ;  men 
who  were  not  likely  to  be  impressed  by  any  but  the 
most  solid  and  striking  of  arguments.  He  was  lis- 
tened to  by  all  with  equal  delight  and  profit,  and 
after  a  few  days,  three  youths  of  the  university,  who 
had  received  the  degree  of  bachelor,  moved  by  the 
I         discourse  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  entered  religious

houses,  one  becoming  a  Dominican,  and  the  two

Once  when  he  was  going  to  preach  in  a  town 
belonging  to  the  bishopric  of  Segorbe,  he  said  on 
the  road  to  his  companions :  "  Three  several 
times  already  has  there  been  an  intention  of  call- 
ing us  to  preach  in  the  town  whither  we  are  going, 
but  the  devil  has  always  prevented  it,  (God  so 
permitting)  this  time,  however,  the  fiend  has  not 
succeeded ;  and  I  am  in  hopes  the  divine  word 
will  produce  great  fruit."    And  so  it  did. 

Besides  several  other  conversions,  there  was  one 
very  remarkable  and  edifying.  A  certain  noble 
lady  fascinated  by  a  cavalier,  of  rank  corresponding 
with  her  own,  was  leading  a  very  immoral  life ; 
so  carefully  did  they  conceal  their  delinquencies, 
that  both  of  them  were  looked  upon  as  very 
reputable  persons.  Blessed  Nicholas's  sermons 
did  not  suffice  to  move  this  guilty  lady  to 
sincere  repentance,  though  they  contributed  to- 
wards it.  He  found  means  to  see  her  privately, 
and  by  degrees  gave  her  to  understand  that  he 
knew  the  state  of  her  poor  sinful  soul.  The  lady 
blushed  when  she  found  herself  discovered  by  the 
servant  of  God ;  and  being  convinced  that  our 
Lord  had  thus  miraculously  enlightened  him  for 
the  sake  of  her  salvation,  she  became  penitent, 
made  her  confessions  with  marks  of  extraordinary 
contrition,  began  a  new  life,  and  persevered  in 
it  till  her  death ;  similar  in  this  to  Mary  Mag- 
dalen, the  sinner  of  the  Gospel,  with  the  exception 
that  whereas,  the  sins  and  penance  of  the  saints 
were  matters  of  public  notoriety,  those  of  the

contrite  and  weeping,  she  turned  back,  made  her 
confession,  and  did  penance  for  her  previous  irre- 
gularities. 


CHAPTER  IV. 

REMARKABLE  CIRCUMSTANCES  CONNECTED  WITH  THE 
PREACHING  OP  BLESSED  NICHOLAS. 

It  seems  to  me  that  our  Lord  was  pleased  to 
glorify  the  preaching  of  Blessed  Nicholas  in  a  very 
unusual  manner.  Frequently  in  the  course  of  his 
sermons  he  was  ravished  in  God,  and  remained 
in  an  ecstasy  for  a  long  time ;  at  other  times  his 
body  was  raised  in  the  air  in  the  presence  of  a 
numerous  auditory.  I  am  not  aware  whether  the 
same  thing  is  recorded  of  any  other  saint.  We

378 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE, 


shall  write  more  at  large  elsewhere  on  these  ecs- 
tasies of  our  saint ;  merely  touching  here  on  that 
which  occurred  when  he  was  in  public.  Preach- 
ing at  Valencia  in  the  church  of  the  Blessed  Tri- 
nity on  the  festival  of  S.  Mary  Magdalen,  he 
spoke  of  divine  charity,  when  his  face  suddenly 
became  inflamed ;  he  was  perceived  to  be  strug- 
gling, as  it  were,  for  some  time  against  the  at- 
traction of  the  Supreme  Good ;  but  at  length  he 
went  off  in  an  ecstasy,  becoming  immoveable  and 
wholly  absorbed  in  God,  remaining  so  till  the  end 
of  the  divine  offices. 

Another  time,  as  he  was  preaching  in  the 
church  of  S.  Thomas  at  Valencia,  he  fell  into  au 
ecstasy,  and  was  for  a  long  time  immoveable  in 
the  pulpit.  Three  persons  of  high  rank  were  so 
struck  at  this  sight,  that  becoming  penitent  they 
changed  their  lives,  made  their  confessions,  and 
from  sinners,  as  they  then  were,  they  became  exem- 
plary christians. 

In  the  parish  church  of  the  town  of  Oliva,  where 
he  was  preaching,  he  had  gone  through  a  great  part 
of  his  sermon,  when  he  suddenly  went  into  an  ecs- 
tasy, and  he  remained  in  that  state  in  the  pulpit 
till  the  solemn  mass  was  quite  finished.  His  com- 
panions ran  a  needle  into  his  foot  whilst  he  was 
in  this  state  of  ecstasy,  but  it  did  not  arouse  him, 
nor  did  he  feel  the  slightest  pain  at  the  time. 

Whilst  he  was  at  Valencia,  he  used  to  go  and 
preach  at  a  place  frequented  by  public  sinners ; 
once  as  he  was  addressing  these  unfortunate 
creatures,  he  fell  into  an  ecstasy  of  long  dura- 
tion :  to  prove  the  extent  of  his  abstraction,  and

see  how  far  his  sensibilities  were  deadened,  an 
indiscreet  man  drove  a  thick  needle  into  his  leg 
and  left  it  sticking  in  the  flesh.  Niccolo  felt 
nothing  at  the  time,  but  after  his  ecstasy,  as  he

One  Wednesday  in  holy  week,  as  he  was  preach- 
ing in  the  church  of  S.  Catherine  of  Sienna,  on 
the  agony  of  our  Lord  in  the  garden  of  Geth-

something  more  than  human,  he  began  to  say : 
"Jesus  Christ  the  Son  of  God,  essentially  holy, 
prays,  suffers,  and  sweats  blood  from  excess  of 
grief,  whilst  Brother  Nicholas,  a  grievous  sinner, 
enjoys  delight,  inebriated  with  the  Sovereign 
Good  !"  These  words  drew  tears  from  the  whole 
audience.  On  returning  to  his  ordinary  state,  and 
seeing  the  contrite  emotion  of  the  people,  he  said, 
14  What,  brethren,  are  you  still  waiting  for  me  ? 
God  will  reward  your  patience  ;  a  new  life,  a  new 
book  ;  thus  do  I,  the  greatest  of  sinners,  promise  !" 
whereupon  the  tears  and  sighs  of  the  people  were 
redoubled.  Having  finished  his  sermon,  and 
quitted  the  pulpit,  he  raised  his  eyes  to  the  cruci- 
fix, went  off  again  into  an  ecstasy,  standing  in  the

deeply  affected,  and  burst  forth  in  a  strain  of  ten- 
der contrition :  a  great  crowd  began  to  collect 
round  him,  so  to  prevent  his  being  stifled  ;  a  num- 
ber of  vigorous  men  were  obliged  to  raise  him

in  their  arms,  break  a  passage  through  the  crowd, 
and  carry  him  along,  he  being  all  the  time  in  an

He  was  extraordinary  confessor  to  the  nuns  in 
Valencia,  and  was  at  their  convent  one  day  when 
there  was  a  procession  of  the  Blessed  Sacrament, 
he  himself  carrying  the  monstrance  ;  on  reaching 
the  steps  of  the  altar,  he  began  a  discourse  on  the 
love  which  Jesus  bore  to  his  beloved  disciple  S. 
John ;  he  spoke  with  so  much  unction,  that  the 
whole  audience  began  to  weep  with  devotion ;  he 
himself  became  immoveable  and  ecstatic  ;  uncon- 
sciously to  himself  the  Blessed  Sacrament  was 
taken  out  of  his  hands,  and  replaced  in  the  taber- 
nacle, and  he  remained  in  his  ecstasy  till  late  at 
night.  On  recovering  from  these  ecstasies  in  the 
pulpit,  it  was  remarkable  that  he  always  resumed 
his  discourse  precisely  where  he  had  come  to  a  stop. 
In  one  of  these  ecstasies  he  was  seen  with  his 
whole  body  raised  in  the  air. 

He  had  a  great  devotion  to  the  infant  Jesus ; 
hence  almost  every  year  his  fellow-religious  made 
him  preach  on  Christmas  eve,  and  on  these 
occasions  he  generally  fell  into  an  ecstasy,  and 
sometimes  remained  so  from  the  morning  of  the 
vigil  till  midnight.  In  one  of  these  long  ecstasies 
he  predicted  great  and  terrible  future  events, 
which  were  afterwards  fully  verified. 

Besides  these  ecstasies,  he  was  seen  by  many 
people  with  rays  of  light  issuing  from  his  face 
and  whole  person  when  he  was  preaching ;  and

than  a  quarter  of  an  hour,  during  which  time  the 
birds  remained  where  they  were  without  stirring, 
and  in  the  attitude  of  attentive  listeners. 


CHAPTER  V. 

BLESSED  NICHOLAS  IS  MADE  GUARDIAN. 

His  sermons,  from  the  applause  they  created,  and 
the  amazing  fruit  which  everywhere  and  in  all 
classes  resulted  from  them,  rendered  the  name 
of  Blessed  Nicholas  famous  throughout  the  pro- 
vince of  Valencia.    His  superiors  had  no  idea  of 


Digitized  by  Google 


382 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


withdrawing  him  from  this  important  ministry, 
but  felt  convinced  that  he  was  fully  competent 
to  the  double  task  of  government  and  preaching. 
In  the  year  1548  a  chapter  of  the  order  was  held 
at  Valencia,  when  Nicholas  was  elected  guardian 
of  the  conveut  called  Valle  di  Gesu,  very  retired 
and  of  very  strict  observance  ;  it  was  situated  at 
about  three  miles  distance  from  Valencia.  In 
proportion  as  every  one  else  rejoiced  at  this  elec- 
tion, he  was  most  deeply  afflicted.  He  repre- 
sented to  his  superiors  his  too  great  youth  and  his 
inability  to  govern  ;  he  found  numberless  demerits 
in  himself,  to  which  he  added  tears  and  entreaties, 
that  he  might  be  dispensed  from  an  obedience  so 
oppressive  to  him.  His  superiors  gave  him  no  other 
answer  than  that  he  ought  calmly  to  submit  to  the 
dispensations  of  Divine  Providence.  With  holy 
indifference  of  mind,  but  with  a  great  hope  of 
being  heard,  he  remained  in  the  choir  after  com- 
plin, on  the  vigil  of  the  Ascension,  and  began  to 
beseech  Almighty  God  to  relieve  him  from  the 
burden  of  superiority.  After  praying  for  some 
time  with  extraordinary  fervour,  he  was  raised  in 
ecstasy,  wholly  absorbed  in  God.  The  father  com- 
missary-general and  the  others  in  the  convent  or 
S.  Maria  di  Gesu,  where  the  chapter  had  been 
held,  were  informed  of  it,  and  all  hastened  to  the 
choir  to  look  at  Niccolo,  whom  they  found  with 
a  face  like  that  of  an  angel,  insensible  to  all  cor- 
poral objects,  and  immoveable,  with  the  exception 
that  now  and  then  he  struck  his  breast,  and  sweetly 
said  these  words,  "My  heart  is  ready,  0  God, 
my  heart  is  ready."    He  continued  in  this  ecs-

tasy  till  the  morning  of  the  Ascension,  when 
mass  being  ended,  he  went  to  father  cominissary 
and  father  provincial,  and  told  them  with  great 
simplicity  that  he  submitted,  and  consented  to  fill 
the  office  of  guardian.  This  convinced  them  that 
God  had  signified  His  will  to  him  in  some  extra- 
ordinary manner.  The  results  of  his  government

expectation.  When  superior,  he  made  not  the 
slightest  change  in  his  mode  of  life,  with  the  ex-

exact  of  all  in  the  observance  of  the  rules,  to  take 
upon  himself  the  greatest  share  of  toil,  and  to  make 
himself  in  all  things  the  servant  of  all  the  reli- 
gious committed  to  his  charge.  It  is  inconceiv- 
able with  what  care  and  assiduity  he  saw  that 
none  of  his  subjects  were  left  without  those  ne- 
cessaries and  little  conveniences  permitted  by  the 
rule  and  poverty  of  S.  Francis,  or  the  exquisite 
delicacy  with  which  he  attended  to  their  wants, 
and  this  during  the  whole  time  that  he  was  su- 
perior, which  was  for  many  years.  In  the 
different  monasteries  in  which  he  governed,  he 
knew  how  to  maintain  perfect  peace  and  mutual 
charity  amongst  the  brethren,  inspiring  a  filial 
confidence  in  all  of  them  towards  himself,  so  that 
they  freely  had  recourse  to  him  in  all  their  ne- 
cessities, both  spiritual  and  temporal.  He  loved 
them  all,  not  only  with  a  father's,  but  with  a  mo- 
ther's love ;  each  one  of  them  felt  persuaded 
that  he  was  loved  by  him,  as  much  as  if  he  alone 
enjoyed  all  the  affection  and  all  the  solicitude  of 
this  good  father.

He  was  the  first  in  the  choir  and  at  all  other 
duties  of  the  community.  At  recreation  he  was 
the  most  cheerful  of  all,  and  instead  of  allowing 
his  rank  to  impose  anything  like  importunate  sub- 
jection on  the  rest,  his  familiar  affability  of  man- 
ner, his  amusing  jokes  and  simple  hilarity,  con- 
tributed to  make  every  one  happy  and  cheerful 

He  was  most  zealous  on  the  point  of  strict 
regularity,  but  with  the  utmost  discretion,  pru- 
dence, and  charity.  He  overlooked  no  failings, 
but  he  corrected  and  punished  with  such  judicious 
gentleness,  that  even  his  very  corrections  con- 
vinced the  delinquents  that  they  were  sincerely 
loved  by  their  saintly  father. 

He  was  guardian  of  several  houses  for  many 
years ;  he  was  likewise  the  definitor  of  the  pro- 
vince, and  all  the  witnesses  who  were  examined 
in  the  processes  for  his  canonization,  attested  that 
his  method  of  government  had  ever  been  perfect, 
as  far  as  is  possible  in  man  ;  that  he  was  loved 
and  revered  by  his  subjects,  that  he  was  ever 
careful  to  promote  the  deserving,  and  to  keep 
back  those  who  were  not  so,  that  on  this  point 
he  could  neither  be  moved  by  the  love  or  fear  of 
any  one,  and  that  he  encountered  contradictions 
and  trials,  neither  few  nor  trifling  on  this  very 
account. 

In  the  year  1556  Blessed  Nicholas  was  guardian 
of  the  monastery  of  S.  Francis  di  Chelva.  The 
whole  province  of  Valencia  was  then  afflicted  with 
a  deplorable  scarcity  of  provisions,  and  the  alms 
on  which  our  religious  depended  were  not  too 
abundant ;  Nicholas,  however,  insisted  that  every

highly  edified  by  the  kindness,  charity,  and  virtue

In  addition  to  the  affliction  of  the  existing 
scarcity  in  Valencia,  there  was  every  reason  to 
apprehend  still  greater  misery :  there  had  been 
several  months  of  dry  weather ;  the  seeds  already 
sown  had  not  as  yet  appeared  above  ground,  nor 
was  there  a  possibility  of  planting  those  which  were 
still  unsown.  Blessed  Nicholas  in  his  frequent 
sermons  urged  the  people  to  appease  the  anger 
of  the  Lord  :  several  pious  processions  were  made, 
and  prayer  and  fasting  went  on  for  many  days. 
Notwithstanding  all  this,  there  was  not  the  slight- 
est sign  of  rain.  One  day  he  preached  to  the 
people  with  extraordinary  fervour ;  they  were 
profoundly  moved,  and  abundant  were  the  tears 
they  shed  ;  long  and  ardently  did  they  implore 
the  Divine  succour  in  this  their  present  necessity. 
Nicholas  encouraged  them  to  persevere  in  prayer, 
tenderly  reminding  them  of  the  infinite  goodness 
of  God,  and  of  the  sweet  and  paternal  charity  with 
which  He  loves  us:  "let  us,  0  my  brethren," 
said  he,  "rest  in  the  affectionate  arms  of  our 
Almighty  and  Divine  Father,  and  let  us  hope 
that  He  will  soon  console  us."  On  returning  to 
his  convent,  he  assembled  his  religious,  made 
them  a  powerful  and  fervent  exhortation,  be- 
seeching them  to  unite  altogether  in  renewing 
their  supplications  to  God,  under  the  present 
threatening  calamities,  recommending  them  to 
second  their  prayers  by  mortification,  by  each  one 
giving  himself  a  severe  discipline.  This  was 
done;    many  scourged   themselves  to  blood;

Blessed  Nicholas  more  than  all  the  rest.  At  that

CHAPTER  VL 

HE  IS  MADE  MASTER  OF  NOVICES. 

The  exalted  sanctity  of  Nicholas,  who  by  this 
time  was  famed  and  revered  throughout  the  whole 
province  of  Valencia,  his  perfect  discernment  of 
spirits,  as  we  shall  show  in  its  proper  place,  and 
above  all,  his  admirable  prudence  and  talent  in 
the  direction  of  souls,  determined  his  superiors 
to  appoint  him  master  of  novices  in  the  con- 
vent of  S.  Francis  at  Valencia.  During  the  time 
that  he  told  this  office,  he  had  always  twenty, 
two  or  more  novices  under  him,  who  all  declared 
that  they  had  ever  found  him  an  accomplished 
model  of  evangelical  perfection,  according  to 
the  spirit  of  8.  Francis  ;  to  be  such,  he  had 
nothing  else  to  do  but  to  continue  what  he 
had  all  along  been.  He  loved  his  spiritual  chil- 
dren with  a  stronger,  sweeter,  and  more  sincere 
affection  than  their  natural  parents  could  have 


Digitized  by  Google 


388 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


felt  for  them.  When  necessary,  he  corrected 
and  punished  them  as  the  rule  directed,  with 
so  much  efficacy,  yet  with  so  much  charity, 
that  even  in  his  very  chastisements,  the  youths 
acknowledged  the  love  of  their  holy  father,  and 
were  grateful  to  him  for  it.  He  exercised  his 
novices  in  every  virtue,  especially  in  humility, 
the  characteristic  virtue  of  our  holy  father  S. 
Francis,  as  it  must  likewise  be  that  of  all  his  true 
children.  The  better  to  instruct  his  novices  in 
this  great  virtue,  he  relied  on  example  rather  than 
on  words.  Frequently  did  he  collect  his"  novices 
around  him,  and  then  with  deep  shame  and  grief, 
he  told  them  that  he  was  a  great  hypocrite,  who 
by  his  deceit  imposed  on  his  religious  brethren 
and  on  the  world ;  that  under  specious  appear- 
ances, he  in  reality  transgressed  all  the  constitu- 
tions and  rules  of  the  order  ;  and  that  if  men  did 
but  know  his  sins,  they  would  abhor  and  execrate 
him  as  they  would  a  fiend  from  hell.  After  this 
he  ordered  each  of  his  novices  to  reprehend  him 
severely  for  some  vice,  telling  them  they  need  not 
fear  making  a  mistake  in  their  selection,  because 
all  vices  dwelt  in  him.  Such  a  command  as  this 
was  always  most  distressing  to  these  good  youths, 
nevertheless  they  were  obliged  to  obey  as  best  they 
could.  To  every  fault  that  he  was  accused  of,  he 
answered  that  in  truth  he  was  guilty  of  it ;  and 
with  tears  in  his  eyes  and  compunction  in  his 
heart,  he  begged  pardon  of  God,  of  his  novices, 
and  of  every  one  else.  As  soon  as  each  one  of  his 
pupils  had  accused  and  reproached  him  on  the 
score  of /such  and  such  faults,  he  imposed  another

order  on.  them  no  less  painful  than  the  first ;

consent  to  this,  but  said  with  a  sigh :  "  If  you  and 
others  did  but  know  my  great  malice,  you  would

He  had  several  times  admonished  and  corrected

other  religious  were  extremely  edified  and  affected. 

Besides  all  this,  he  constituted  one  of  the 
novices  superior  over  him,  often  going  to  him  to 
accuse  himself  of  some  fault,  a  fault  which  could 
only  seem  such  to  his  heroic  humility,  after  which, 
the  novice  was  to  impose  a  penance  ;  in  this  prac- 
tice he  had  to  suffer  from  indiscretion,  simplicity, 
and  even  from  a  fervour  which  was  not  according 
to  knowledge  and  truth ;  though  such  as  would 
reasonably  be  expected  in  these  juvenile  superiors. 
These  practices  of  humility  are  to  be  admired, 
not  to  be  imitated,  unless  the  person  be  impelled 
by  an  extraordinary  spirit  of  the  Lord,  as  was  the 
case  with  Blessed  Nicholas.     That  in  him  this

CHAPTER  VII. 


HE  IS  APPOINTED  CONFESSOR  OF  NUNS. 

From  want  of  authentic  documents  I  am  unable 
to  specify >the  precise  year  when  Blessed  Nicholas 
was  appointed  by  his  superiors  to  the  spiritual 
direction  of  the  nuns  subject  to  our  order;  nor 
can  I  positively  name  the  various  convents  in 
which  he  discharged  this  function.  We  know  for 
certain  that  he  was  confessor  to  the  ladies  of  the

NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


royal  convent  of  the  Discalsced  at  Madrid,  and 
must  have  been  one  of  the  first  thus  engaged,  as 
we  find  him  mentioned  as  confessor  there  in  the

Joanna  of  Austria;  it  also  seems  certain  that

from  it. 

In  the  convent  of  S.  Glare,  at  Gandia,  there  was 
a  young  nun  called  Anna  of  the  Conception,  who 
had  taken  the  habit,  and  had  been  professed  against 
her  will ;  hence  she  was  unhappy  in  her  state, 
feeling  a  repugnance  to  every  thing,  and  to  every 
duty  of  the  community  ;  being  a  person  of  great 
self-control,  she  concealed  her  feelings  so  far  as  to 
appear  happy  and  regular ;  so  much  so,  that  the 
other  nuns  looked  upon  her  as  one  of  the  hap- 
piest amongst  them.  For  a  long  time  she  had 
besought  our  Lord  to  free  her  from  the  distressing 
repugnance  she  felt  towards  a  state  and  duties  to 
which  she  was  irrevocably  and  irremediably  bound ; 
her  disgusts,  however,  became  daily  more  keen 
and  bitter :  and  yet  there  was  no  one  to  whom  she 
could  disclose  her  torture.  It  seems  to  me,  that 
a  young  lady  who  studied  to  comply  exactly  with 
all  the  duties  prescribed  by  the  Franciscan  rule 
(in  spite  of  her  natural  repugnances),  and  who 
earnestly  prayed  to  be  relieved  from  those  repug- 
nances, who  strove  not  only  to  be  a  religious,  but

CHAPTER  VIII. 

CONTINUATION  OF  THE  SAME  SUBJECT. 

The  many  extraordinary  graces  by  which  God 
was  pleased  to  manifest  the  sanctity  of  Blessed 
Nicholas  to  the  world,  contributed  immensely  to 
the  success  of  his  labours  in  behalf  of  his  neigh- 
bour, and  rendered  him  famous  as  a  director  of 
religious  communities.  Not  once  only,  but  as 
we  may  almost  say,  continually,  was  he  seen  by 
the  nuns  (whose  confessor  he  was)  in  a  state  of 
ecstasy;  and  we  may  easily  imagine  the  bene- 
ficial effects  which  the  sight  of  their  saintly  con- 
fessor in  ecstasy  would  naturally  produce  on  the 
minds  of  his  penitents.  Whilst  he  was  confessor 
to  the  nuns  of  S.  Clare,  in  the  town  of  Sciativa, 
now  called  S.  Flippo,  he  once  entered  the  con- 
fessional to  hear  the  nuns,  but  went  off  in  an 
ecstasy  almost  immediately,  and  remained  in  it 
four  hours,  and  spoke  with  extraordinary  fervour, 
and  with  a  sublimity  superior  to  all  the  lights  of 
human  learning. 

In  the  confessional  belonging  to  the  nuns  of 
the  Blessed  Trinity  in  Valencia,  he  had  so  re- 
markable an  ecstasy,  that  they  supposed  him  to 
be  taken  dangerously  ill,  and  called  in  medical 
aid.

As  ho  was  hearing  the  confession  of  a  nun  at 
Gandia,  she  perceived  him  all  at  once  go  off  in 
an  ecstasy ;  she  herself  at  the  same  time  felt 
an  ardent  love  enkindled  within  her,  drawing  her 
to  God  in  an  irresistible  manner.  She  attentively 
watched  the  countenance  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  so 
strongly  betraying  the  sweet  miracles  of  divine 
charity ;  at  one  time  it  was  tearful,  and  expres- 
sive of  deep  anguish  ;  then  again  it  became  ra- 
diant and  joyous  ;  thus  continually  alternating 
from  pain  to  pleasure.  The  nun  was  distressed 
and  alarmed  at  this  sight,  and  as  soon  as  the 
ecstasy  was  ended,  she  besought  him,  in  the 
name  of  Jesus  Christ,  to  explain  the  meaning  of 
the  joy  and  grief  depicted  in  his  countenance 
during  his  ecstasy.  With  ingenuous  simplicity, 
he  replied  :  "  I  cannot  refuse  your  request,  made 
in  the  name  of  our  most  amiable  Jesus.  In  my 
ecstasy  I  saw  our  Blessed  Lady,  who  placed  her 
divine  Son  on  my  bosom  ;  as  I  pressed  the  Infant 
Jesus  in  my  arms,  I  seemed  to  taste  the  joys  of 
Paradise,  and  this  made  me  look  so  cheerful. 
At  the  same  time,  however,  I  saw  my  own  malice, 
which  pressed  on  my  heart  like  the  pains  of  hell  ; 
this  will  account  for  the  grief  you  witnessed." 

One  holy  Thursday,  when  he  was  confessor  in 
the  before-named  convent  of  the  Blessed  Trinity, 
he  sung  the  solemn  mass,  communicated  all  the 
nuns,  made  the  usual  procession,  and  deposited  the 
Blessed  Sacrament  on  the  altar  of  the  sepulchre, 
after  which,  with  the  sacred  vestments  still  on  him, 
he  became  immovable  at  the  steps  of  the  said  altar, 
and  was  wholly  absorbed  in  God  in  one  of  the  most

several  books,  presenting  passages  in  them  to

with  which  the  Spanish  Inquisition  decided  such

as  the  number  of  persons  who  were  discovered 
and  punished  for  affected  sanctity ;  so  that  when 
a  learned  and  cautious  inquisitor,  after  a  long 
private  examination,  at  once  declared  the  ecsta-

was  a  great  saint,  it  seems  to  me  that  this 
is  a  remarkable  and  significant  demonstration  that 
God  would  have  the  merits  of  His  faithful  servant 
both  known  and  glorified. 

From  this  time,  then,  the  high  opinion  and 
veneration  of  all  classes  towards  him  was  such  as 
could  scarcely  be  surpassed.  Philip  II.  and  all 
the  royal  family  honoured  him  exceedingly  ;  the 
highest  nobles  continually  had  recourse  to  him. 
The  heroic  humility  of  Blessed  Nicholas  could  not 
endure  this  honourable  distinction  ;  but  he  knew 
no  means  of  escaping  from  it,  unless  he  secretly 
fled  from  Madrid,  and  returned  to  his  monastery 
of  S.  Maria  di  Gesil  at  Valencia ;  accordingly  he 
did  so.    On  leaving  the  capital,  he  stopped  at  the

CHAPTER  X. 

FRIENDSHIP  BETWEEN  S.  LEWIS  BERTH  AND  AND 
BLESSED  NICHOLAS.  SOME  EVENTS  CONNECTED  WITH 
THE  DEATH  OP  THE  FORMER. 

Soon  after  Blessed  Nicholas's  return  from 
Madrid  to  Valencia,  S.  Lewis  Bertrand,  of -the 
illustrious  order  of  S.  Dominic,  departed  this  life. 
This  great  saint,  after  sanctifying  Spain  by  his 
preaching  and  example,  went  on  the  American 
missions,  from  whence,  by  the  dispensation  of 
Providence,  he  returned  to  Valencia,  his  native 
place,  towards  the  end  of  the  year  1569.  Nicho- 
las, who  was  then  at  Valencia,  went  to  visit  his 
fellow  townsman,  who  was  highly  esteemed  for 
his  sanctity :  they  conversed  together  on  spiritual 
matters  with  great  fervour,  when  at  once  Blessed

their  mutual  esteem  augment,  each  one  looking

CHAPTER  XI. 

HE  JOINS  THE  CAPUCHINS. 

After  the  death  of  S.  Lewis  Bertrand,  the  fame 
of  this  wonderful  ecstasy  raised  the  veneration 
of  the  city  of  Valencia  for  Blessed  Nicholas  to 
the  highest  pitch  ;  so  to  escape  from  the  honours 
lavished  on  him  by  men,  he  solicited  and  obtained 
the  consent  of  superiors  to  repair  to  Catalonia, 
and  join  the  Capuchins.  The  better  to  explain 
this  step,  we  may  observe  that  at  the  time  we 
write  the  Capuchins  did  not  form  a  totally  dis* 
tinct  body  from  the  Observantines,  so  that  with 
the  simple  license  of  superiors,  the  latter  could 


Digitized  by  Google 


414 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE, 


pass  over  to  the  Capuchins,  then  considered  as  a 
strict  reform  of  the  Minors.  The  desire  of  greater 
perfection,  and  the  delusive  hope  of  living  un- 
known in  the  kingdom  of  Catalonia,  determined 
him  to  take  this  step,  though  Divine  Providence 
had  ordained  otherwise.  All  that  Blessed  Nicholas 
gained  thereby  was  censure,  and  accusations  of 
levity  from  those  who  are  ever  apt  to  blame  what 
they  do  not  understand  ;  at  all  events,  it  was  the 
will  of  God  that  he  should  be  glorified  amongst 
the  Capuchins,  and  in  whatever  parts  of  Catalonia 
were  visited  by  him,  even  more  so  than  in  Valencia 
and  amongst  the  Observantines,  Scarcely  had  he 
set  out  on  his  journey  to  Catalonia,  and  reached 
the  territory  of  Alcora,  than  Don  John  Bertrand, 
rector  of  the  place,  went  forth  with  other  priests 
to  meet  him.  Nicholas  had  stopped  at  the  house 
of  a  pious  benefactor  of  the  Franciscans,  and 
without  the  slightest  intimation  being  given  him,  he 
said,  "  Let  us  go  and  meet  the  Reverend  Rector, 
who  is  coming  to  visit  us."  On  meeting  him  and 
his  companions,  he  called  Don  John  by  his  proper 
name,  as  if  they  were  old  acquaintances,  at  which 
every  one  was  much  astonished.  The  rector 
would  have  him  and  his  companions  lodge  in 
his  house ;  and  for  several  days  after  the  room 
in  which  Nicholas  slept  retained  quite  a  heavenly 
fragrance.  A  Dominican  who  had  been  preaching 
the  Lent  at  Alcora  travelled  in  company  with 
our  saint,  and  having  a  pair  of  scissors,  he  eagerly 
watched  for  an  opportunity  of  clipping  off  a  bit  of 
his  habit  unperceived  by  Nicholas,  intending  to 
keep  it  as  a  relic,  but  the  latter  said  to  him  with

a  smile,  "  Father,  you  may  as  well  pack  up  your 
scissors,  for  you  will  not  be  able  to  do  what  you 
intend.' ' 

On  his  arrival  at  Tortosa,  be  could  not  refuse 
to  preach  in  the  principal  church,  which  he  did 
in  presence  of  an  immense  concourse*  of  people, 
and  with  great  fruit.  In  the  middle  of  his  sermon 
he  exclaimed  with  great  emphasis,  and  to  the 
terror  of  every  one,  "  Tortosa !  Tortosa !  oh, 
what  a  dreadful  chastisement  hangs  over  thee ! 
Oh,  how  near  it  is  at  hand !"  In  a  very  short 
time  the  river  rose  immoderately,  and  overflowing 
in  all  directions,  ravaged  both  town  and  country, 
carrying  away  houses,  trees,  flocks,  and  herdsmen, 
so  that  the  territory  of  Tortosa  was  little  better 
than  a  desert ;  in  addition  to  this,  several  manu- 
factories in  the  city  were  materially  damaged. 

On  reaching  Falcetta,  ho  was  taken  to  see  a 
sick  woman  whose  life  was  despaired  of ;  he  made 
the  sign  of  the  cross  on  her  forehead,  and  said  a 
Gospel  from  S.  John,  when  she  immediately  grew 
better,  and  was  soon  perfectly  cured. 

The  nuns  of  Scornalbou,  in  the  diocese  of 
Tortosa,  much  wished  him  to  make  them  a  little 
spiritual  discourse,  sitting  in  a  chair  in  their 
church;  it  was  found  necessary  to  admit  some 
seculars  as  well  as  the  religious.  He  spoke  admi- 
rably, and  in  the  middle  of  his  discourse  fell  into 
an  ecstasy :  on  recovering  himself,  he  resumed 
his  subject  just  where  he  had  left  off;  he  ad- 
dressed the  seculars  individually,  calling  each  one 
by  his  own  name,  specifying  each  one's  occupa- 
tion, and  telling  each  one  what  he  must  do  in 


Digitized  by  Google 


416 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


order  to  be  saved.  We  may  imagine  the  uni- 
versal astonishment,  and  how  much  all  would  be 
animated  to  persevere  in  the  ways  of  the.  Lord. 
As  Blessed  Nicholas  had  never  seen  any  of 
them  before,  they  were  convinced  that  the  things 
he  had  told  them  could  only  have  been  known  by 
him  in  a  supernatural  manner.  In  almost  every 
place  he  accosted  the  people  who  went  to  speak 
to  him  by  their  proper  names,  as  if  they  were 
familiarly  known  to  him. 

He  reached  the  hermitage  of  the  Madonna 
di  Riva  corvera  in  July,  on  the  eve  of  S.  Marga- 
ret's day,  when  there  was  a  solemn  anniversary 
for  the  dead  of  that  nermitage.  Our  saint  assisted 
at  the  solemn  mass,  and  then  fell  into  an  ecstasy  on 
his  knees  before  the  altar  of  the  Blessed  Sacra- 
ment. He  rose  as  if  out  of  himself,  in  a  state  of 
excessive  joy,  and  shortly  afterwards  said  to  all 
the  people  who  were  round  him,  "Do  you  know 
what  it  is  that  makes  me  thus  blithe  and  happy  ? 
yes,  I  have  seen,  I  have  seen  S.  Francis  and  S. 
Dominic,  with  S.  Lewis  Bertrand  between  them ! 
O,  what  immense  glory !  O,  what  inexplicable 
grandeur!  O,  what  ineffable  joy!  We  do  not 
all  wear  the  same  habit  in  this  world,  but  the 
spirit  of  charity  is  the  same  in  all ;  we  are  all 
beloved,  and  doubly  beloved  brethren  in  Jesus 
Christ." 

If  I  undertook  to  narrate  all  the  remarkable 
incidents  which  occurred  during  Blessed  Nicholas' 
journey  to  Barcelona  to  assume  the  garb  of  the

CHAPTER  XII. 

HIS  RETURN  TO  THE  OBSERV  ANTINES. 

As  yet  I  have  found  no  authentic  document 
to  show  the  precise  date  when  Blessed  Nicholas 
put  on  the  Capuchin  habit.  He  certainly  wore 
it  but  a  short  time,  since  he  did  not  quit  Valencia 
until  April  1582 ;  before  he  went  to  Barcelona, 
where  he  joined  the  Capuchins,  he  spent  some 
time  amongst  the  Recoliectines,  and  on  the  23rd  of 
June,  1583,  he  laid  aside  the  Capuchin  habit. 
These  changes  occurred  within  a  few  months,  and 
in  the  last  year  of  the  saint's  life ;  they  gave  rise 
to  many  remarks  at  the  time  they  occurred,  and 
to  many  difficulties  and  objections  to  the  Postula- 
tes of  his  cause,  as  well  as  to  the  ecclesiastics 
who  were  appointed  to  examine  his  virtues.  It  is 
certain  (and  the  Church  has  so  decided)  that  in 
all  this  he  was  moved  by  the  Spirit  of  God,  which 
breathes  where  and  as  it  will ;  nor  can  man  of 
himself  understand  either  its  source  or  its  par- 
ticular and  immediate  aim ;  certainly,  however, 
27  .

as  the  first  principle  proceeds  from  God,  so  too 
does  the  end  conduce  to  Him.  When  Blessed 
Nicholas  was  asked  bj  many  the  cause  of  these 
unlooked  for  changes,  he  merely  answered  that 
he  could  not  do  otherwise  than  follow  the  will  of 
God ;  that  the  mode  of  life  prescribed  by  the 
rules  of  the  Observantine  was  holy,  so  was  that 
of  the  Recollectine  Fathers,  so  was  that  of  the 
Capuchins,  so  was  that  of  all  other  religious 
orders  approved  by  the  Church.  From  this  pru- 
dent answer  of  his  we  may  safely  conjecture, 
that  our  Lord,  with  a  view  of  keeping  regulars 
steady  in  their  vocation,  and  in  the  order  to 
which  He  first  calls  them,  was  pleased  to  permit 
this  sort  of  inconstancy  in  one  of  His  servants 
who  had  reached  a  most  heroic  degree  of  evan- 
gelical perfection,  by  placing  him  first  amongst  the 
Observantine  Minors,  then  with  the  Recollectine, 
then  with  the  Capuchins,  and  lastly,  with  the 
Observantines  again:  being  everywhere  equally 
favoured  with  miraculous  gifts,  and  greatly  glo- 
rified in  the  sight  of  men.  We  know  for  cer- 
tain, that  in  the  days  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  sev- 
eral religious,  in  other  respects  edifying  enough, 
passed  over  to  other  orders,  under  the  pretext  of 
reform  or  of  stricter  regularity,  or  else  joined  one 
of  the  new  orders  which  then  arose ;  and  that 
these  said  religious  were  terribly  assailed  by  the 
devil  on  the  point  of  their  original  vocation ;  the 
consequence  was,  that  some  joined  institutes  of 
which  the  austerities  were  far  beyond  their  strength, 
and  soon  became  unequal  even  to  the  mildest 
rules ;  whilst  others,  deluded  by  the  same  tempta-

tion,  forsook  the  religious  state,  and  returned  to

On  his  arrival  at  Barcelona,  the  corporation  of 
the  city  went  in  a  body  to  welcome  him  in  the 
name  of  the  public,  and  to  express  the  gratifica-

amongst  them.  He  was  horrified  at  such  a  com- 
pliment; he  threw  himself  on  the  ground  in  a 
flood  of  tears,  exclaiming,  "  These  compliments  to 
the  greatest  sinner  in  the  world  I  Am  I,  an  exe- 
crable sinner,  to  be  esteemed  and  praised  with  so 
much  goodness  ?"  This  incident  tells  the  opinion 
in  which  he  was  held  at  Barcelona  at  his  first 
appearance  there  ;  we  may  imagine,  then,  how 
astonished  and  edified  those  public  functionaries 
would  be  by  his  sanctity,  and  by  his  unexpected 
humility  on  this  occasion.  Soon  after  this  some 
distinguished  ladies  and  gentlemen  of  the  city 
called  upon  him;  amongst  others,  the  wife  of 
Viscount  d'  Evoli.  Nicholas  went  down  to  the 
church  door  to  speak  to  them ;  after  discoursing 
a  while  on  the  things  of  God,  he  fell  into  an 
ecstasy,  and  remained  suspended  in  the  air  for 
about  half  an  hour. 

Scarcely  had  the  Capuchin  fathers  given  him 
their  habit,  than  superiors  were  obliged  to  let  him 
preach  in  different  churches  in  Barcelona,  being 
asked  by  persons  who  could  not  be  refused*  To- 
wards the  end  of  his  sermon  in  the  church  of

S.  Justus,  he  told  his  audience  that  the  ador-

During  his  stay  in  Barcelona,  he  scarcely  ever 
entered  a  pulpit  without  being  rapt  in  ecstasy, 
when  crowds  often  saw  him  raised  more  than  a 
palm  from  the  ground,  and  remain  so  for  a  long

Owing  to  all  these  prodigies,  every  one  wished 
to  speak  to  our  saint ;  every  parish  would  have 
him  preach  in  their  church,  so  that  the  house  of 
the  Capuchin  fathers  was  besieged  by  persons  of 
the  highest  rank  as  well  as  by  others ;  his  supe- 
riors were  often  puzzled  how  to  decide,  when  sev- 
eral different  parties  wanted  him  on  the  same 
day.  He  was  often  asked  whether  such  crowds  of 
people,  taking  up  his  time  from  morning  till  night, 
together  with  such  incessant  preaching,  did  not 
distract  his  prayer;  he  answered  with  humble 
simplicity,  that  on  the  contrary  it  kept  him 
habitually  united  with  the*  Sovereign  Good  in 
calm  continual  prayer.  But  as  this  strict  union 
with  God  is  only  granted  to  the  greatest  saints,  it 
must  be  admitted  that  this  perpetual  influx  of 
strangers  interfered  very  much  with  the  prayer, 
recollection,  and  solitude  of  the  Capuchin  fathers ; 
although  they  highly  delighted  in  having  amongst 
them  so  great  a  saint,  such  a  model  of  consum- 
mate perfection,  according  to  the  spirit  of  the

seraphical  father  S.  Fraacis ;  they  deemed  it 
expedient,  nevertheless,  to  use  all  the  means  they

Blessed  Nicholas,  finding  it  impossible  to  attain 
the  obscure  and  hidden  life  amongst  the  Capu-

Observantines,  with  the  consent  of  the  superiors

To  give  some  idea  of  the  esteem  in  which  he 
was  universally  held,  we  may  state  that  when  he 
resumed  the  habit  of  the  Observantines,  the  bar-

beard  with  great  devotion,  and  distributed  it  as 
relics  to  many ;  after  his  death,  several  miracles 
were  wrought  by  means  of  it;  amongst  others, 
the  very  religious  who  had  shaved  him,  after  joy- 
ously blessing  himself  with  this  relic,  was  instan- 
taneously freed  from  a  quartan  fever  which  had 
troubled  him  for  several  months. 


CHAPTER  XIII. 

HIS  RETURN  TO  VALENCIA. 

Many  miraculous  events  signalized  Blessed 
Nicholas's  return  from  Barcelona  to  A  Valencia, 
which  took  place  shortly  before  his  death,  as  is 
attested  in  the  processes ;  but  as  these  deposi- 
tions are  not  chronologically  arranged,  we  cannot 
specify  their  precise  dates.   It  seems  probable

NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


and  almost  certain,  that  in  this  journey  from 
Barcelona  to  Valencia,  he  stopped  at  Tarragona, 
of  which  Antonio  Agostini  was  then  archbishop, 
a  model  for  ecclesiastical  pastors,  a  bright  lumi- 
nary of  sacred  and  profane  literature  in  every 
branch.  This  excellent  prelate  was  acquainted 
with  our  saint,  whom  he  highly  esteemed  as  a 
holy  man,  and  as  one  according  to  God's  own 
heart ;  and  one  whom  God  in  His  mercy  wonder* 
fully  glorified.  As  soon  as  he  heard  of  his  arri- 
val at  Tarragona,  he  immediately  sent  for  him, 
insisting  that  he  should  stay  and  dine  with  him, 
together  with  several  other  learned  and  pious 
priests ;  such  only  being  admitted  to  the  friend- 
ship and  familiarity  of  this  most  worthy  arch- 
bishop. Blessed  Nicholas  found  the  party  quiet 
according  to  his  own  heart;  the  repast  was  in 
every  respect  worthy  of  one  of  the  highest  ecclesi- 
astics of  the  church  of  Spain ;  the  conversation 
of  the  archbishop  and  his  guests  was  cheerful  aud 
agreeable,  yet  learned  and  religious.  Towards 
the  end  of  dinner,  the  archbishop,  who  had  placed 
Nicholas  beside  him,  told  him  that  he  should  very 
much  like  to  hear  him  sing,  as  he  knew  that  he 
was  a  musician ;  the  holy  man  at  once  consented ; 
whereupon  the  archbishop  summoned  his  Maestro 
di  Capella,  and  several  of  his  young  pupils.  They 
began  to  sing  the  psalm  "Laudate  pueri  Do- 
minum;"  and  at  the  second  verse,  "Blessed  be 
the  name  of  the  Lord,"  Nicholas  rose  from  his 
seat,  his  countenance  beaming,  and  sparkling 
with  divine  love,  and  remained  for  a  long  time 
immoveable,  with  his  eyes  closed,  in  a  state  of

profound  ecstasy.  It  would  be  impossible  to  des-

In  memory  of  so  exalted  and  sublime  an  ecs- 
tasy, of  which  he  himself  had  been  a  witness, 
this  pious  prelate  had  the  above  lines  set  to 
music,  and  took  pleasure  in  hearing  them  sung ; 
moreover  he  had  the  music  and  words  printed, 
so  that  any  one  might  sing  them  who  wished  to 
do  so. 

On  reaching  Cabanes,  in  the  province  of  Valen- 
cia, Blessed  Nicholas  was  lodged  in  the  house  of 
John  Gavalda,  a  public  notary,  who  was  affiliated 
to  the  order  of  S.  Francis,  and  who  always  gave 
a  welcome  to  the  religious  who  had  occasion  to 
pass  through  Cabanes.  Our  saint  paid  the  follow- 
ing pretty  and  consoling  compliment  to  his  pious 
host:  "My  dear  little  brother,  you  welcome  to 
your  house,  and  you  give  food  to  the  poor  of  Jesus

Christ,  that  is,  to  the  poor  sons  of  S.  Francis  who 
pass  this  way,  and  God  will  receive  you  into  His 
celestial  home,  where  you  will  for  ever  feast  at  the

nothing  to  any  one,  but  I  am  now  returning  to 
Valencia,  and  when  I  shall  have  again  beheld  it, 
I  shall  in  a  few  days'  time  cease  to  live  in  this 
poor  world,"  The  holy  death  of  Blessed  Nicholas 
occurred  a  few  days  later  ;  and  we  may  imagine 
how  surprised,  and  at  the  same  time  how  consoled 
the  notary  and  his  sister  were,  to  whom  he  had  so 
clearly  and  so  cheerfully  foretold  his  approaching 
end.
