fortified  with  the  holy  oils ;  answering  to  all  the 
usual  prayers  of  the  church.  Every  one  wished 
to  be  present  at  his  last  passage,  which  seemed 
close  at  hand  ;  they  remained  therefore  in  the  sick 
man's,  or  in  the  adjoining  rooms.  Blessed  Nicholas 
again  entreated  the  Father  Guardian  to  have  him 
buried  in  some  vile  place,  as  being  so  great  a  sin- 
ner, wholly  unworthy  of  being  buried  amongst  the 
religious.  Father  Guardian  again  told  him  he 
would  do  his  duty,  and  that  he  should  be  satisfied. 
He  requested  the  religious  to  retire  to  rest,  leaving 
him  with  two  Fathers  whom  he  named  ;  and  then 
to  return  if  they  pleased  in  the  morning,  to  help 
him  with  their  prayers  in  his  passage  to  eternity. 
Accordingly  they  all  left  him,  excepting  the  two 
he  had  asked  for. 

He  begged  they  would  from  time  to  time  pro- 
nounce the  holy  names  of  Jesus  and  Mary,  and 
recite  the  Apostles'  creed  aloud  to  him.  About 
the  middle  of  the  night,  one  of  the  religious,

NICHOLAS  FOTORE. 


429 


whose  room  was  at  no  great  distance  from  the  in. 
firmary,  heard  strains  of  delightful  music,  ap- 
parently proceeding  from  the  chamber  of  Blessed 
Nicholas ;  he  hastened  thither,  and  found  that 
the  sounds  of  many  instruments  seemed  to  issue 
from  the  top  of  his  bed  :  he  and  the  two  religious 
who  were  watching  by  the  dying  man,  listened 
with  delight  to  the  heavenly  strains.  They  looked 
round  the  house,  and  out  of  the  windows,  to  dis- 
cover whether  the  music  was  from  without,  but  deep 
silence  reigned  everywhere ;  therefore  the  three 
were  convinced  that  the  music  they  heard  was 
supernatural  and  angelical ;  that  in  fact,  it  was  a 
foretaste  of  paradise  afforded  the  holy  man  in  his 
last  agony  ;  if  that  can  be  called  agony  which, 
seemed  to  be  so  inexpressibly  joyful.  The  dying 
saint  reclined  on  his  bed  with  a  cheerful  coun- 
tenance, his  mind  wholly  absorbed  in  God  ;  in  fine, 
in  a  state  of  ecstasy.  The  three  religious  were 
conversing  together  about  this  miraculous  har- 
mony, when  Blessed  Nicholas  turned  his  eyes  to- 
wards them,  and  said  with  a  smile,  "  Hush  !  my 
very  dear  brothers,  hush !"  and  immediately  re- 
turned to  his  state  of  ecstasy.  Morning  came, 
and  with  it  every  symptom  of  his  last  hour.  The 
usual  sign  was  given,  and  all  the  religious  hastened 
to  join  in  the  recommendation  of  the  departing 
soul ;  with  a  feeble  voice,  he  joined  with  the  rest 
in  these  most  devout  prayers  of  the  church  :  which 
being  ended,  his  dying  eyes  brightened  up,  he 
cast  an  affectionate  look  upon  his  crucifix,  then 
humbly  closed  his  eyes,  and  without  a  movement 
of  any  kind,  he  said  "Jesus!  I  believe!"  and

placidly  expired  on  the  morning  of  the  twenty- 
third  of  December,  1583,  on  a  Friday,  aged  63 
years,  five  months,  and  twenty-five  days,  having 
lived  in  the  Order  of  S.  Francis  forty-six  years 
and  a  few  days. 


CHAPTER  XV. 

HIS  OBSEQUIES  AND  BURIAL. 

When  Blessed  Nicholas  was  dead,  Dr*  Lewis 
Almenara,  lecturer  of  medicine  in  the  University 
of  Valencia,  repaired  to  the  monastery  of  S. 
Maria  di  Gesu.  He  was  highly  celebrated,  and 
had  been  called  in  by  the  doctors  during  the  ill- 
ness of  the  saint.  He  wished  to  examine  the  body 
minutely :  he  found  the  limbs  flexible,  the  flesh 
soft  and  healthy,  just  as  if  he  were  alive  ;  he  per- 
ceived likewise  a  slight  moisture  of  extremely 
pleasant  odour.  He  pointed  out  these  circum- 
stances to  the  religious,  positively  declaring  that 
these  appearances  were  in  his  opinion  miraculous, 
and  beyond  the  order  of  nature.  His  death  was 
kept  secret  till  the  next  morning,  when  his  body 
was  carried  into  the  church.  The  Dominicans  im- 
mediately hastened  thither  in  procession,  to  assist 
at  his  obsequies.  As  soon  as  his  death  became 
known,  the  whole  of  Valencia  was  in  commotion  ; 
and  before  the  obsequies  were  over,  many  distin- 
guished persons  began  to  cut  off  portions  of  his 
habit,  to  be  kept  as  relics  ;  the  concourse  round 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE, 


431 


the  holy  body  became  so  great,  and  their  pious 
rapacity  so  unsparing,  the  habit  and  hair  being 
clipped  in  all  directions,  that  as  soon  as  the  obse- 
quies were  over,  the  body  was  conveyed  into  a 
small  chapel,  where  it  could  be  seen,  but  not 
touched  by  the  people.  Without  this  precaution 
popular  devotion  would  have  entirely  despoiled  it. 
The  religious  were  anxious  to  bury  him,  but  this 
was  found  to  be  impossible,  and  he  remained  ex- 
posed in  the  little  chapel  for  nine  days.  The  Pro- 
vincial, seeing  so  much  excitement  in  the  city, 
appointed  solemn  obsequies  to  be  celebrated  in  the 
church  of  S.  Francis,  on  the  morning  of  holy  Inno- 
cents' day.  All  the  religious  orders  came  hither 
processionally,  as  well  as  vast  crowds  of  people 
of  all  ranks.  A  panegyric  was  delivered  on  his 
heroic  virtues,  which  was  listened  to  by  all  with 
edification  and  delight ;  people  took  pleasure  in 
referring  to  it ;  especially  those  who  had  been 
best  acquainted  with  him.  In  the  mean  time, 
the  church  where  his  body  remained  exposed  was 
seldom  or  ever  empty  ;  and  though  the  winter  of 
that  year  was  particularly  mild  and  damp,  the 
body  daily  became  more  beautiful,  seeming  to  the 
spectators  like  a  person  in  a  sweet  and  tranquil 
slumber.  Moreover,  it  exhaled  a  most  delicious 
fragrance,  impregnating  the  rosaries  and  other 
things  which  out  of  devotion  were  applied  to 
it;  many  of  these  objects  retained  this  plea- 
sant scent  even  for  months.  And  although, 
generally  speaking,  the  church  was  full  from 
morning  till  night,  not  the  slightest  unpleasant 
odour  was  perceptible,  which,  naturally  speaking,

NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


ought  to  have  heen  the  case :  on  the  contrary, 
the  before-mentioued  fragrance  remained  unal- 
loyed. This  was  unanimously  declared  to  be  a 
miracle.  Some  persons  suspected  and  hinted  that 
the  body  must  have  been  embalmed,  which  ac

night  following  the  last  day  of  the  year.  Before 
the  burial,  however,  he  would  have  it  legally  re- 
cognised by  public  and  competent  judges,  leaving 
documents  to  show  that  the  body  of  the  holy  man 
had  never  been  opened,  but  was  intact,  and  had 
remained  healthy  and  flexible  up  to  the  ninth  day, 
the  delicious  odour  remaining  unabated.  All  this 
was  carried  into  effect ;  after  which,  the  body  was 
respectfully  enclosed  in  a  coffin,  with  the  usual 
formality  of  seals,  inscriptions,  &c,9  and  was 
then  buried  in  a  place  apart,  during  the  night  of  the 
31st  December,  1583,  in  the  church  belonging  to 
the  monastery  of  S.  Maria  di  Gesu,  where  he  had 
taken  the  habit  of  S.  Francis,  where  he  had  lived 
for  many  years,  where  he  died,  and  where  his  re- 
mains now  rest  and  are  preserved. 


CHAPTER  XVI. 

M1BCLES  AT  HIS  DEATH. 

As  in  life  so  likewisie  n  death  would  our  Lord 
render  Blessed  Nicholas  glorious.  I  think  I  may 
be  allowed  to  say  with  truth,  that  through  his 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


433 


means  and  intercession,  the  blind  recovered  their 
sight,  the  deaf  hearing,  the  languid  strength, 
lepers  were  cleansed,  the  crooked  made  straight, 
every  sort  of  complaint  was  cured,  and  even  the 
dead  restored  to  life.  Nor  let  me  here  be  accused 
of  irreverence,  unworthy  of  a  Catholic  historian, 
for  presuming  to  apply  to  Blessed  Nicholas  that 
eulogium  which  Christ  our  Lord  the  Son  of  God 
applied  to  Himself  and  His  own  miracles.  Every 
Christian  knows  that  the  power  of  working  mir- 
acles is  the  peculiar  attribute  of  Jesus  Christ, 
who  performs  them  by  His  own  might ;  whereas 
in  His  saints  it  is  but  a  gift,  when,  by  their 
means,  the  divine  power  of  Jesus  acts ;  hence 
the  miracles  of  the  saints  are  His  works,  He 
having  declared  that  in  His  Church  His  servants 
should  accomplish  the  same  prodigies  as  He  Him- 
self had  wrought  during  His  mortal  life,  nay,  even 
greater  still. 

Father  Christopher  Moreno,  the  intimate  and 
confidential  friend  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  was  pro- 
vincial of  the  Observantines  of  Valencia  at 
the  time  of  his  death ;  moreover,  he  was  then  in 
Valencia,  and  was  examined  in  the  processes  for 
his  beatification ;  this  learned  and  pious  religious 
man  was  the  first  who  wrote  and  published  the 
Life  of  Blessed  Nicholas  a  few  years  after  his 
precious  death  ;  eight  chapters  of  his  history  were 
taken  up  with  narrations  of  the  miracles  which 
occurred  after  his  death,  and  through  his  inter- 
cession; they  amount  to  about  a  hundred,  to 
which  may  be  added  a  still  greater  number  which 
have  taken  place  since  Father  Moreno  published

Father  Francis  Stella,  who  heard  his  confession 
in  his  last  illness,  was  reciting  the  office  of  our 
Lady  in  his  own  room  very  early  in  the  morning 
of  Christmas  Eve,  that  is,  the  morning  after 
Blessed  Nicholas's  death.  The  father  fell  into 
a  slumber,  during  which  he  saw  Father  Jerome 
Esteve  (one  of  the  religious  who  had  recently  died 
in  a  well  founded  opinion  of  high  sanctity,)  who 
distinctly  told  Father  Francis  that  Blessed  Nicho- 
las was  already  in  heaven,  and  in  great  glory : 
hereupon  Father  Francis  awoke,  and  found  him- 
self environed  with  light  which  filled  the  whole 
room;  he  was  at  first  alarmed,  fearing  some 
illusion  of  the  devil ;  he  made  the  sign  of  the 
cross  several  times,  and  closed  his  eyes,  that  he 
might  not  see  the  light,  recommending  himself 
earnestly  to  God  and  to  our  Blessed  Lady.  After 
a  time  he  began  to  suspect  that  possibly  this 
great  light  might  be  meant  to  signify  Purgatory, 
and  that  the  soul  of  Father  Nicholas  might  be 
in  those  flames,  in  need  of  prayers.  At  length 
he  opened  his  eyes  again,  and  still  found  his 
room  filled  with  so  brilliant  a  light,  that  the 
brightness  of  the  sun  could  bear  no  proportion 
to  it;  at  the  same  time  his  whole  soul  seemed 
wrapped  in  soft  composure,  with  a  kind  of  positive 
conviction  that  Blessed  Nicholas,  so  far  from 
being  in  purgatory,  had  attained  to  heavenly  glory ; 
afterwards,  he  saw  this  marvellous  light  ascend 
by  little  and  little  to  heaven,  until  at  last  he 
quite  lost  sight  of  it ;  he  himself  experienced  a

feeling  of  great  comfort,  and  he  was  moreover

the  ways  of  the  Lord.  During  Christmas  night,

He  celebrated  his  masses  with  unusual  fervour,,

unconsciously  ejaculated,  "Saint  Nicholas,  pray

ful light,  more  bright  than  the  sun,  between  him- 
self and  the  chalice ;  it  remained  there  beneath

During  the  same  Christmas  night,  a  pious 
widow  of  Valencia,  who  was  ill  in  bed,  recom-

Scarcely  had  she  finished  this  prayer,  than  she

with  much  benevolence  he  began  to  speak  to  her

not  die  of  that  illness ;  he  exhorted  her  to  pa-

better  to  sustain  her  great  and  painful  trials,  and

apparition,  which  lasted  a  considerable  time,  the 
sick  woman  felt  much  consoled,  and  with  an 
ardent  desire  of  suffering. 

On  the  same  Christmas  day,  a  religious  of  the 
monastery  of  S.  Maria  di  Gesit  was  in  a  dying

all  his  members  recovered  their  natural  power,  he 
rose  from  his  bed,  and  went  down  to  the  church

On  the  same  day,  a  lady  of  Valencia  was  sudden- 
ly cured  of  a  rupture,  from  which  she  had  been 
suffering  for  eleven  years,  and  this  after  merely 
recommending  herself  piously  to  Father  Nicholas. 

Donna  Maria,  the  wife  of  Don  Christopher 
Mercador,  had  a  complaint  in  her  left  eye  of  four 
months'  standing ;  she  had  tried  all  the  remedies 
proposed  by  the  most  skilful  doctors  and  surgeons 
of  the  day,  but  all  in  vain ;  and  as  the  complaint 
daily  grew  worse  and  worse,  every  one  feared  that 
the  poor  lady  would  lose  her  eye.  On  the  day  of 
Father  Nicholas's  funeral,  she  went  to  the  church 
of  S.  Maria  di  Gesu,  approached  the  holy  body,  and 
respectfully  taking  one  of  the  hands,  she  applied  it 
to  her  diseased  eye  with  lively  faith  ;  at  that  very 
moment  the  pain  ceased,  and  the  eye  was  restored 
to  a  better  condition  than  it  had  been  in,  even 
before  it  was  affected. 

A  newly-married  young  man  of  Valencia, 
named  Esteve,  fell  ill  of  a  slow  fever  soon  after 
his  nuptials ;  he  was  declared  consumptive,  and 
received  the  holy  Viaticum  and  Extreme  Unction 
sixteen  days  after  the  death  of  Blessed  Nicholas. 
The  afflicted  mother  of  the  young  man  went  to 
the  church  of  the  Dominicans,  to  recommend  her 
dying  son  to  S.  Vincent  Ferrer  and  S.  Lewis 
Bertrand,  and  on  her  return  home,  to  her  surprise 
and  delight,  she  found  her  son  sleeping  tranquilly. 
After  some  time  he  awoke,  apparently  in  high 
spirits,  and  asked  his  mother  how  many  days  there

About  the  same  time,  and  in  the  same  city,  our

that  the  gentleman  would  take  it  in  good  part,

Michael  Crespo,  who  belonged  to  the  retinue  of

beheld  Blessed  Nicholas,  who,  seating  himself  at 
his  bed  side,  began  to  comfort  him  with  indescri-

Frances  Fernandez  fell  ill  of  a  putrid  fever,

Nicholas,  are  sufficient  for  our  present  purposes. 


CHAPTER  XVII. 

THE  FAME  OF  HIS  SANCTITY — HIS  BEATIFICATION. 

The  fame  of  Blessed  Nicholas's  exalted  sanctity 
had  resounded  throughout  the  kingdom  of  Spain, 
but  after  his  holy  death  it  increased  marvellously, 
and  became  universal  in  the  church  of  Jesus 
Christ.  S.  Lewis  Bertrand  when  alive  had  spoken 
highly  of  him,  as  was  attested  in  the  processes  by 
the  very  persons  who  had  gathered  the  words 
from  the  lips  of  S.  Lewis  himself.  He  was  held 
in  terms  of  equal  veneration  by  Don  John  di 
Ribera,  archbishop  of  Valencia,  who,  amongst

444

many  similar  things,  said  to  Blessed  Nicholas  on 
the  occasion  of  the  great  concourse  of  people  who 
bad  assembled  at  the  solemn  obsequies  of  the 
before-named  S.  Lewis,  "Father  Nicholas,  we 
shall  see  the  same  numerous  assembly,  the  same 
tender  devotion  and  compunction  in  Valencia 
when  you  die."  S.  Paschal  Baylon,  who  survived 
our  saint  some  years,  continually  spoke  of  the 
miraculous  events  connected  with  Father  Nicholas 
Fattore.  Leaving  all  the  rest,  three  such  wit- 
nesses as  these  sufficed  to  fill  the  whole  catholic 
world  with  the  name  and  fame  of  Blessed  Nicho- 
las.

keeping ;  and  here  he  remained  long  kneeling  in 
fervent  prayer.  He  and  his  party  would  next 
visit  the  infirmary,  where  the  holy  man  had  died ; 
after  viewing  and  honouring  the  walls,  the  poor 
bed  from  whence  he  had  flown  to  heaven,  and  the 
habit  he  had  worn,  which,  since  his  death,  had 
been  left  extended  on  the  bed,  (the  whole  being 
piously  cherished  by  the  religious  of  the  house) 
his  majesty  blessed  God,  the  Giver  of  all  good 
gifts,  for  what  he  had  there  seen  and  heard.'  The

indeed  surprising  that  his  beatification  should

should  have  been  prolonged  for  two  centuries,

delay.  Perhaps  the  loving  providence  of  our  Lord 
may  have  deferred  glorifying  and  raising  Blessed 
Nicholas  Fattore  to  the  honour  of  our  altars  till  the 
present  time,  in  order  to  confound  modern  free-

Catholics ;  for  the  peculiar  characteristic  of  Blessed 
Nicholas's  sanctity  is  diametrically  opposite  to 
the  vices  and  errors  of  our  days ;  and  it  is  by  a 
beneficent  dispensation  of  the  Most  High,  that 
Pius  VI.,  so  fervently  zealous  as  he  was  in  sup- 
porting  the  truths  of  divine  revelation  against  the 
sophistries  of  modern  libertinism,  should  present 
this  great  model  to  the  whole  Church,  that  it 
might  everywhere  produce  fruits  of  Christian  fer- 
vour and  piety.  Solemn  canonization  must  yet 
complete  the  religious  honours  already  awarded 
to  Blessed  Nicholas  Fattore,  by  means  of  which 
he  will  be  immortalized  in  the  memory  of  all  the 
true  followers  of  Jesus  Christ,  and  throughout  the 
Church  to  the  end  of  time. 


CHAPTER  XVIII. 

THE  MIRACLES  APPROVED  FOR  HIS  BEATIFICATION. 

According  to  the  decrees  of  Pope  Urban  VIII., 
only  two  miracles,  approved  as  such  by  the  Sacred 
Congregation  of  Rites,  were  necessary  for  the 
Beatification  of  Nicholas  Fattore ;  nevertheless, 
three  were  proposed,  and  all  three  were  approved 
by  the  said  congregation  and  by  Pope  Pius  VI.,

John  Baptist  Claudi,  a  child  thirteen  months 
old,  being  left  near  the  door  of  the  house,  by  some 
means  crawled  out  into  the  middle  of  the  street ; 
it  so  happened  that  a  great  fourwheeled  cart 
heavily  laden  passed  along;  one  of  the  front

several  people,  leaving  him  either  dead  or  dying ; 
the  frantic  mother  flew  to  raise  her  infant,  and 
found  him  not  only  torn  in  several  different 
places,  but  with  a  severe  contusion  on  the  loins, 
surrounded  by  a  deep  scar,  partly  red  and 
partly  black.  The  unfortunate  woman  held  the 
child  (dead  as  every  one  believed)  tightly  pressed 
upon  her  breast,  standing  there  like  a  statue, 
senseless  and  immoveable.  After  gazing  thus 
with  a  fixed  and  stupid  eye  upon  her  child  for 
some  time,  she  raised  her  eyes  to  heaven,  exclaim- 
ing with  lively  faith,  "  Father  Nicholas,  I  recom- 
mend my  own  life  and  the  life  of  my  child  to 
thee ;  I  here  claim  him  at  your  hands  alive  and 
well,  as  God  gave  him  to  me,  and  as  He  khas 
hitherto  preserved  him.  I  will  carry  him  in 
devotion  to  your  tomb,  and  there,  through  your 
hands,  I  will  offer  him  to  the  Almighty."  Several 
persons  surrounded  the  mother,  and  they  all  im- 
plored Blessed  Nicholas's  succour  for  the  child. 
Scarcely  was  this  done,  than  the  babe  raised  his 
drooping  head,  and  with  bright  eyes  smiled  upon 
his  mother,  nestling  himself  more  closely  to  her 
bosom.  Not  only  was  he  alive  and  well,  but 
every  sign  of  the  accident  bad  disappeared,  to

Jerome  Espeso  practised  medicine  at  Moya,  in 
the  kingdom  of  Castile.  One  night  when  he  was 
at  home,  he  heard  loud  cries  for  help  proceeding 
from  a  neighbouring  street ;  a  priest,  a  relative 
of  his  own,  was  attacked  by  one  who  bore  him 
ill-will.  Jerome  ran  to  the  assistance  of  the 
priest,  succeeded  in  separating  the  two,  and  ap- 
peased the  dispute  which  had  arisen  between 
them ;  the  exasperated  aggressor,  however,  aimed 
his  dagger  at  Jerome,  inflicting  a  deep  wound  in 
his  breast.  He  was  conveyed  home,  where,  on 
examination,  the  wound  was  declared  mortal,  and 
his  death  apparently  was  close  at  hand ;  he  imme- 
diately made  his  confession,  and  received  the  holy 
Viaticum  and  Extreme  Unction.  On  the  following 
morning  a  messenger  was  dispatched  to  Valencia, 
to  summon  a  very  celebrated  surgeon  belonging 
to  that  city.  He  proceeded  to  Moya,  and  pro- 
nounced the  wound  to  be  extremely  dangerous, 
adding,  that  if  Jerome  survived  it,  he  would  re- 
quire long  and  constant  care.  As  he  could  not 
remain  at  Moya,  after  dressing  the  wound,  he 
had  the  wounded  man  very  gently  conveyed  back 
with  him  to  Valencia.  Great  and  excellent  as 
were  the  care  and  skill  of  the  surgeon,  the  wound 
grew  worse ;  a  bard  substance  formed  round  the

edge  of  it,  aad  increased  daily,  in  spite  of  all

the  tomb  of  his  blessed  deliverer.

patronage  of  our  saint.

BOOK  II. 


CHAPTER  I. 

OP  HIS  VIRTUES. — HIS  HEROIC  FAITH. 

Haying  detailed  in  as  good  order  as  I  could 
the  various  incidents  connected  with  the  life  and 
actions  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  it  now  remains  for  me 
to  treat  more  at  large  on  the  subject  of  his  vir- 
tues, setting  forth  those  acts  which  show  them  to 
be  heroicaL  In  the  first  place,  let  us  speak  of 
Faith,  which  is  the  first  that  God  infuses  into 
man  in  his  justification ;  it  is,  moreover,  the  first 
virtue  which  in  man,  prevented  and  aided  by 
grace,  produces  effects. 

Whilst  yet  a  child  of  only  five  or  six  years  old, 
he  recognized  Jesus  Christ  in  the  person  of  poor 
leprous  beggars,  whom  he  relieved,  and  whose 
wounds  he  kissed,  saying,  and  showing  by  his 
deeds,  that  he  gave  food  to  Jesus  through  them, 
and  kissed  His  wounds  in  theirs.  These  offices 
of  charity  to  the  poor  were  habitual  in  Blessed 
Nicholas  during  the  whole  course  of  his  life ;  and 
they  can  only  have  proceeded  (especially  in  his 
childhood)  from  his  lively  faith.  Blessed  Nicho- 
las was  very  learned ;  he  was  constantly  em- 
ployed in  the  ministry  of  preaching,  neverthe-

less  with  heroic  faith,  he  made  his  chief  pre- 
paration for  his  sermons  consist  in  extraordi- 
nary prayer,  fasting,  and  other  austerities:  in 
effect,  frequently  this  was  his  sole  preparation 
for  preaching,  and  yet  the  generality  of  the  peo- 
ple were  astonished  at  the  depth  of  learning  he 
displayed,  as  well  as  his  power  of  moving 
even  the  most  obdurate  and  abandoned  sinners. 
In  all  his  sermons  and  familiar  discourses  he 
ever  spoke  of  things  belonging  to  the  Catholic 
religion,  in  a  manner  which  showed  his  full  and 
entire  adhesion  to  every  maxim  of  the  faith,  and 
to  every  mystery  which  it  inculcates;  so  that 
every  one  could  perceive  how  thorough  was  his 
conviction  of  its  truth,  a  conviction  more  sincere 
and  solid  than  he  had  of  things  palpable  and 
evident  to  the  senses. 

This  lively  persuasion  of  the  maxims  of  our 
holy  faith  gave  rise  to  his  almost  daily  ecstasies^ 
in  one  of  which  he  spoke  at  large  of  the  inesti- 
mable favour  which  our  Lord  confers  on  those 
servants  whom  He  chooses  to  bear  witness  to  the 
truth  of  His  holy  Gospel,  by  the  effusion  of  their 
blood  by  means  of  martyrdom.  He  continually 
declared  that  he  bore  a  holy  envy  to  the  martyrs 
of  Jesus  Christ,  and  to  those  religious  who  went 
to  preach  the  faith  in  infidel  countries  ;  often  did 
he  petition  his  superiors  to  send  him  into  Africa, 
that  he  might  labour  in  the  conversion  of  the 
infidels,  hoping  that  he  might  there  meet  with  a 
cruel  death,  in  defence  of  the  faith  of  Jesus  Christ. 
Although  this  request  was  invariably  refused,  it 
is  inconceivable  with  what  zeal  and  ardour  he

strove  to  convert  the  few  mahoraedans  who  lived 
in  the  province  of  Valencia.  By  a  special  inspi-

The  devils  often  appeared  to  him  under  terrible

permits  the  power  of  the  devil  to  be  superior  to 
His  divine  assistance,  and  that  God  would  enable 
him  to  triumph  over  all  his  attacks  ;  by  the  light 
of  this  truth  he  felt  no  fear  under  the  many  great 
assaults  to  which  he  was  subjected  by  the  devil, 
but  from  which  he  always  came  forth  with 
increased  merits.  He  drew  up  on  paper,  written 
by  his  own  hand,  and  with  his  own  blood,  an 
explicit  confession  of  faith,  specifying  all  its  fun- 
damental dogmas  with  wonderful  depth  and  learn- 
ing ;  and  to  prove  his  fervent  and  sincere  attach- 
ment to  the  faith  of  Jesus  Christ,  he  wrote  these 
dogmas  in  the  figure  of  a  human  heart,  likewise 
drawn  in  his  own  blood.

church  has  authoritatively  declared)  that  Blessed

Nicholas  possessed  all  the  principal  Christian  vir-

CHAPTER  II. 

HIS  HEROIC  HOPE. 

Divine  faith  cannot  reach  a  heroic  degree  in 
any  man,  whose  mind  is  not  fully  convinced  that 
God  is  his  only  good,  and  that  nothing  can  be 
good  which  does  not  proceed  from  God,  and  which 
is  not  a  participation  of,  and  a  gift  from  God.  From 
this  conviction  necessarily  springs  divine  hope, 
whereby  we  look  for,  and  ardently  desire  God 
alone,  and  the  participation  of  God  Himself  and  of 
His  gifts.  This  virtue  shone  forth  in  Blessed 
Nicholas,  even  from  his  childhood.  His  generous 
refusal  in  his  youth  of  the  wealth  and  suitable 
nuptials  offered  him  by  his  father,  preferring  the 
poor  and  humble  life  of  a  Franciscan,  clearly 
proves  that  he  cared  and  wished  for  nothing  but 
the  Sovereign  Good. 

But  leaving  these  and  similar  things,  a  fellow- 
religious,  very  learned,  and  much  addicted  to  prac- 
tices of  piety,  asked  him  one  day  in  confidence 
by  what  means  he  had  obtained  from  God  that 
high  contemplation,  and  those  frequent  ecstasies 
and  raptures  with  which  he  was  favoured ;  with 


Digitized  by  Google 


458 


NICHOLAS  FATTOBE. 


his  usual  candour  and  simplicity  Blessed  Nicho- 
las answered,  that  whilst  he  was  in  the  convent  of 
the  Valle  di  Gesu,  one  day  there  seemed  to  pass 
as  in  a  troop  before  his  eyes,  along  the  edge  of  a 
neighbouring  hill,  all  the  honours  and  all  the  plea- 
sures which  a  man  can  enjoy  in  this  life.  All 
these  transitory  goods  seemed  to  put  on  their  most 
attractive  looks:  after  considering  them  atten- 
tively, he  turned  the  eye  of  his  mind  to  God,  and 
immediately  despised,  trampled  upon,  and  abhorred 
all  worldly  things  as  filthy  mire,  at  the  same  time 
feeling  and  understanding  that  there  was  nothing 
worth  caring  for  but  God  Himself ;  after  this  he 
was  favoured  by  our  Lord  with  a  sublime  contem- 
plation of  divine  things,  as  well  as  with  continual 
ecstasies  and  raptures. 

True  Christian  hope,  so  far  from  being  dismayed 
at,  is  rather  strengthened  by  the  greatest  difficul- 
ties, and  by  the  insuperable  obstacles  it  meets 
with ;  it  renders  man  secure,  and  convinces  him 
that  with  it  he  may  overcome  all  opposition ;  "In 
thy  word  I  will  leap  over  the  wall." 

Later  on,  when  treating  of  his  charity  towards 
his  neighbour,  we  shall  relate  several  incidents 
illustrative  of  the  lively  confidence  which  Blessed 
Nicholas  placed  in  the  assistance  of  Almighty 
God,  and  how  it  enabled  him  to  succeed  in  the 
most  difficult  enterprises. 

The  office  of  superior  was  greatly  opposed 
to  his  humility,  bat  as  soon  as  he  knew  that 
God  required  him  to  accept  the  charge,  he 
promptly  and  generously  submitted,  fulfilling  its 
duties  successfully,  and  for  a  long  time.  His

joining  the  Capuchins,  and  then  again  returning 
to  the  Observantines,  in  a  man  already  aged, 
venerated  in  his  order  and  throughout  Spain, 
would  seem  to  one  who  considers  the  case,  a  most 
arduous  undertaking,  if  not  morally  impossible, 
both  on  the  side  of  superiors  who  had  to  concur 
in  the  arrangement,  as  well  as  the  difficulties  to 
be  encountered  by  the  holy  man  himself ;  how- 
ever, as  he  knew  it  to  be  the  will  of  God,  he 
obeyed,  and  superiors  quietly  acquiesced. 

Omitting  many  details,  we  will  mention  one 
which  is  pleasing  and  most  remarkable.  Don 
Francis,  Duke  of  Arragon,  died  suddenly  in  the 
flower  of  his  age,  at  Segorbe.  Donna  Angela  di 
Cardona,  his  wife,  abandoned  herself  to  the  most 
violent  grief ;  she  remained  in  the  episcopal  palace 
where  her  husband  died,  and  shut  herself  up  in  a 
room,  having  a  small  opening  made  in  the  door 
through  which  she  could  receive  those  things  which 
were  absolutely  necessary ;  she  saw  no  one,  and 
would  not  so  much  as  admit  a  maid-servant  into  her 
room  to  perform  the  most  menial  services.  Such 
strange  proceedings  gave  rise  to  serious  fears  as 
to  the  consequences.  The  bishop  of  Segorbe  and 
many  other  illustrious  personages  had  in  vain  at- 
tempted to  persuade  her  to  change  her  conduct. 
The  Duchess  had  spent  two  months  in  this  lugu- 
brious imprisonment,  when  Blessed  Nicholas  ar- 
rived at  the  convent  of  his  order  in  Segorbe. 
Hearing  of  Donna  Angela's  deplorable  condition, 
he  placed  his  whole  confidence  in  God,  repaired  to 
the  episcopal  palace,  and  asked  to  see  the  Duchess. 
He  was  told  this  was  impossible,  but  with  a  freedom

NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


more  than  human,  he  said  that  he  must  absolutely 
speak  to  the  Duchess,  and  accordingly  proceeded 
to  the  room  in  which  she  was  shut  up :  he  was 
introduced,  whereupon,  with  a  grave  smile,  he 
thus  accosted  her :  "  My  lady  Duchess,  this  is  not 
right ;  your  grief  is  excessive  and  unreasonable ; 
it  hehoves  you  to  moderate  it;  I  am  come  in

her  with  so  much  force  and  unction,  that  the

of  the  blessed  man ;  resigued  herself  humbly  to 
the  divine  dispensation,  and  resumed  an  exem- 
plary mode  of  life  befitting  her  exalted  rank,  and 
creditable  to  her  good  sense. 


CHAPTER  III. 

HIS  HEROIC  LOVE  OF  GOD. 

Christian  perfection  and  sanctity  consist  in 
divine  charity ;  and  a  Christian  is  a  great  saint 
before  God,  in  proportion  as  his  love  for  God  is 
great.  Blessed  Nicholas  never  lost  the  habit  of 
charity  infused  into  him  by  God  at  his  baptism. 
According  to  the  testimony  of  his  confessors,  he 
never  lost  it  by  grievous  actual  sin,  and  grievous 
sin  is  the  only  thing  which  can  deprive  us  of  it. 

He  ever  had  the  greatest  horror  of  mortal  sin, 
and  of  all  the  miseries  to  which  poor  human  life 
is  liable ;  the  most  sensible  and  dreadful  to  him 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


461 


was  the  commission  of  any  mortal  sin.  He  con- 
tinually  protested  that  he  would  rather  die  a 
thousand  deaths  than  commit  one  mortal  sin ; 
continually  did  he  beseech  people,  with  most  hum- 
ble  fear,  to  pray  that  God  would  let  him  die 
rather  than  fall  into  sin.  He  made  a  great  friend 
of  his,  a  very  holy  Carthusian,  promise  to  offer 
this  petition  for  him  to  God  every  day  in  his 
mass ;  the  good  monk  made  the  promise,  and  kept 
it.  From  the  beginning  of  his  noviciate  he  exer- 
cised himself  in  most  fervent  acts  of  divine  love 
in  everything  he  did.  In  familiar  conversation 
with  his  companions,  he  seemed  unable  to  speak 
of  anything  else  than  the  love  of  God  ;  nor  could 
he  drag  himself  away  from  such  of  the  more  pious 
religious  when  they  began  to  talk  upon  the  love 
of  God.  In  all  his  sermons  he  spoke  of  divine 
love,  enkindling  it  in  all  hearts.  In  the  confes- 
sional he  always  recommended  his  penitents  to 
the  practice  of  divine  love.  His  heroic  love  of 
God  was  so  universally  known  in  Spain,  that  it 
was  ^generally  asserted  that  S.  Lewis  Bertrand 
and  Blessed  Nicholas  were  two  of  the  greatest 
saints  then  living  in  the  Church  of  Jesus  Christ ; 
and  that  our  Lord  guided  S.  Lewis  by  the  more 
firm  and  trying  road  of  holy  fear,  and  Blessed 
Nicholas  by  the  more  cheerful  and  more  pleasant 
path  of  holy  love. 

From  this  continual  exercise  of  divine  charity, 
he  at  length  arrived  so  far  as  to  live  on  pure 
love,  that  is  to  say,  all  his  thoughts,  all  his 
affections,  whatever  he  did,  either  interiorly  or 
exteriorly,  was  all  one  continued  act  of  charity  ; 


Digitized  by  Google 


462 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


everything  was  an  act  of  divine  love.  As  we  have 
already  remarked  in  the  first  book,  nothing  di- 
verted his  mind  from  the  thought  of  God,  or  from 
loving  Him  ;  and  the  more  he  felt  himself  excited 
to  divine  love  in  labouring  exteriorly  for  the  good 
of  his  neighbour,  so  much  the  greater  was  his 
recollection  of  mind,  and  so  much  the  more  fer- 
vent was  his  prayer. 

How  perfect  and  intense  this  divine  charity  was 
in  him,  was  visibly  demonstrated  by  many  signs, 
especially  by  his  inflamed  and  beaming  counte- 
nance, which  sometimes  made  him  look  less  like 
a  man  than  a  seraph.  I  will  conclude  this  chap- 
ter with  a  circumstance  connected  with  his  love 
of  God,  which  seems  to  me  peculiar  to  Blessed 
Nicholas.  Frequently,  even  in  the  depth  of  win- 
ter, he  was  unable  to  bear  the  burning  ardours 
of  divine  charity  which  pervaded  his  whole  frame ; 
and  would  go  and  plunge  himself  in  cold  and 
even  frozen  water  ;  contact  with  this  ardent  seraph 
made  all  the  water  of  the  pond  into  which  he 
threw  himself  not  only  warm  and  steaming,  but 
even  bubbling,  as  was  declared  in  the  processes, 
by  several  trustworthy  witnesses. 


CHAPTER  IV. 

HIS  LOVE  OF  JESUS  IN  THE  BLESSED  SACRAMENT 
OF  THE  ALTAR. 

If  Blessed  Nicholas  continually  saw  and  loved 
God  in  everything,  we  may  easily  conceive  what

would  be  his  feeling  towards  the  Blessed  Sacra- 
ment, in  which,  by  a  miracle  of  omnipotence  and 
divine  charity,  God,  made  man  for  love  of  us, 
dwells  constantly  amongst  us.  The  reverence 
and  attention  which  Blessed  Nicholas  showed  when 
in  presence  of  the  adorable  sacrament  were  most 
perfect  ;  and  whenever  he  could,  he  spent  many 
hours  consecutively  before  Jesus  in  the  Blessed 
Sacrament,  engaged  in  making  most  perfect  acts 
of  divine  charity.  He  never  omitted  saying  mass 
even  when  he  was  ill  and  suffering  from  in- 
termitting fever. 

By  way  of  preparation  for  mass,  he  recited  the 
seven  penitential  psalms  together  with  the  prayers, 
and  then  took  a  severe  discipline,  often  to  blood ;  it 
happened  more  than  once  that  the  religious,  moved 
to  compassion,  on  hearing  him  inflict  such  heavy 
blows  on  his  innocent  person,  would  go  and  knock 
at  his  door  under  pretext  of  asking  some  question, 
but  in  reality  for  the  sake  of  putting  an  end  to 
his  self-torture.  He  celebrated  mass  with  such 
fervour  as  to  excite  devotion  in  all  who  assisted 
at  it:  often  did  he  see  Jesus  in  the  form  of  an 
infant  in  the  consecrated  Host;  and  generally 
speaking,  when  he  handled  the  consecrated  Host 
his  fingers  did  not  feel  the  proper  eucharistic  spe- 
cies, but  the  softest  and  most  delicate  human 
flesh,  it  was  on  this  account  that  he  used  to  pre- 
sent his  fore  finger  and  thumb,  which  touched  the 
host,  to  those  who  wished  to  kiss  his  hand,  saying : 
u  Kiss  those  fingers  with  great  respect,  for  they  are 
sanctified  by  real  contact  with  Jesus  Christ  our  Lord 
and  Sovereign  Good."   He  thus  satisfied  his  hu-

mility  and  his  love  for  Jesus  in  the  Blessed  Sa- 
crament at  one  and  the  same  time.  He  several 
times  acknowledged  to  persons  of  authority  and 
piety,  that  every  morning  during  mass,  our  Lord 
filled  his  soul  with  new  and  special  gifts,  and  that 
if  he  were  to  write  down  those  only  which  he  re- 
membered, he  could  fill  several  large  volumes. 
Every  year  during  the  octave  of  Corpus  Christi 
he  seemed  as  it  were  inebriated,  and  out  of  him- 
self, through  excess  of  love,  a  love  which  seemed 
to  compel  him  to  some  exterior  acts,  which,  ac 
cording  to  human  rules,  would  appear  unrea- 
sonable or  indecorus.  Sometimes  when  he  was 
before  the  Blessed  Sacrament,  either  on  the  feast 
of  Corpus  Christi  or  during  the  octave,  he  would 
begin  to  dance  with  vivacity  and  joy,  and  with 
a  thrill  of  devotion  :  whilst  in  this  sort  of  ecstasy 
he  would  take  others  by  the  hand,  saying,  "  Come, 
come,  dear  brother,  let  us  exult  and  rejoice ;  let  us 
dance  before  the  Lord!"  and  he  made  them 
dance  with  him ,  when  they  experienced  tender 
feelings  of  devotion  all  the  time.  One  of  his  reli- 
gious brethren,  a  grave  man,  seeing  him  thus 
dance  before  the  Blessed  Sacrament,  reproved 
him  ;  but  he,  quite  out  of  himself  with  joy  and 
delight,  said,  "  Before  that  God  who  is  so  bountiful 
to  me,  I  willingly  abase  myself,  and  will  always 
abase  myself  more  and  more:"  then  taking  the 
religious  by  the  hand,  he  said  to  him,  "  My  very 
dear  brother,  our  only  Good  likes  us  to  be  joyful 
in  Him  and  for  Him  ;  He,  moreover,  is  pleased  with 
this  pious  chorus,  which  acts  in  His  honour,"  say- 
ing this  he  compelled  him  to  dance  with  him,  and

whilst  he  was  doing  so,  he  felt  his  heart  strongly 
moved  to  devotion  and  love  towards  Jesus  in  the 
Eucharist,  so  that  he  could  not  do  otherwise  than 
own  that  Blessed  Nicholas  was  impelled  by  the 
Divine  Spirit  of  wisdom  and  of  perfect  charity 
when  he  performed  these  marvellous  dances. 

God  was  pleased  to  approve  by  evident  miracles, 
both  the  heroic  perfection  of  our  saint's  love  for 
the  Blessed  Sacrament,  and  the  extraordinary  acts 
which  it  sometimes  gave  rise  to.  We  may  say 
that  for  several  years  he  never  celebrated  mass 
without  an  ecstasy  ;  for  several  years  he  scarcely 
ever  knelt  down  before  the  Blessed  Sacrament, 
or  spoke  of  it,  either  in  public  or  in  private,  with- 
out falling  into  an  ecstasy,  and  being  wholly 
alienated  from  all  sensible  things,  and  this  some- 
times for  several  hours. 

In  a  procession  at  Valencia,  Nicholas  was  carry- 
ing the  Blessed  Sacrament ;  all  at  once  a  flight  of 
birds  formed  a  crown  just  above  the  canopy,  sing- 
ing most  melodiously,  and  steadily  accompany- 
ing the  procession,  their  warbling  notes  harmonis- 
ing beautifully  with  the  ecclesiastical  chant.  He 
was  afterwards  asked  what  birds  they  were }  he 
answered  with  a  smile,  that  they  were  angels, 
come  down  from  heaven  to  honour  their  Divine 
King. 

One  morning  as  he  was  giving  communion  t<o 
the  people,  the  sacred  particles  were  seen  to 
move,  and  as  it  were  to  dance  around  his  fingers, 
to  the  astonishment  and  compunction  of  all  who 
beheld  the  miracle.

CHAPTER  V. 

HIS  HEROIC  LOVE  FOR  HIS  NEIGHBOUR,  ESPECIALLY 
THE  POOR. 

All  men  are  the  living  images  of  God  our 
divine  Father ;  whatever  act  of  charity  we  per- 
form for  any  one,  for  God's  sake,  becomes  an  act 
of  divine  charity.  Jesus  Christ  would  be  recog- 
nized by  us  chiefly  in  the  persons  of  the  poor ; 
therefore,  every  act  of  charity  done  to  the  poor, 
for  love  of  Him  is  accepted  by  Him  as  if  done  to 
Himself.  That  this  love  was  perfect  and  heroic 
in  Blessed  Nicholas,  was  shown  even  in  his  child- 
hood. 

He  usually  went  every  day  after  dinner  to  dis- 
tribute the  remnants  to  the  poor  at  the  door, 
availing  himself  of  the  opportunity  to  exhort  them 
to  patience,  to  say  their  prayers,  to  frequent  the 
•acraments,  &c ;  when  he  had  finished,  he  ar- 
ranged them  in  a  group,  and  kneeling  down, 
kissed  their  feet  with  great  respect.  He  obtained 
leave  of  his  superiors  to  beg  for  the  poor,  and  he 
took  great  delight  in  distributing  whatever  he 
received  amongst  those  who  had  recourse  to 
him. 

One  of  his  brothers,  a  doctor  of  law,  saw  him 
wearing  an  old  ragged  tunic  in  the  depth  of  win- 
ter, so  he  bought  him  a  new  coat  to  wear  under 
his  tunic,  and  prevailed  on  him  to  accept  it.  A 
few  days  after  he  met  a  poor  half-naked  beggar, 


Digitized  by  Google 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


467 


whom  he  took  aside,  and  taking  off  his  new  coat, 
he  put  it  on  the  beggar.  Another  time  he  met 
an  ill-clad  man,  all  shivering  with  cold ;  having 
nothing  else  to  give,  he  took  off  his  cloak,  and 
covered  him  with  that. 

Any  little  delicacy  sent  him  by  his  friends  was 
immediately  made  over  to  the  poor ;  in  fact,  it 
was  only  for  their  sake  that  he  ever  consented 
to  accept  anything. 

Regularly,  when  he  went  to  the  door  to  distri- 
bute the  alms  of  the  monastery,  he  instructed  the 
poor  in  the  Christian  doctrine,  often  examining 
them  in  many  things  necessary  to  be  known  ; 
explaining  the  principal  mysteries  and  maxims 
of  our  holy  faith,  and  then  dismissed  them, 
nourished  both  in  soul  and  body. 

Having  obtained  leave  of  his  superiors,  he  daily 
visited  the  hospitals,  serving  the  poor  sick  in  the 
meanest  offices.  He  washed  their  hands  and  feet, 
combed  their  heads,  shaved  those  who  wanted  it, 
cut  their  nails,  made  the  beds,  and  swept  the 
wards  ;  »he  comforted  all,  spoke  to  all,  served  all 
with  a  love  and  assiduity  that  could  scarcely  have 
been  surpassed  by  a  tender  mother  towards  a 
well-loved  child. 

Whilst  he  was  confessor  to  the  nuns,  his  dinner 
and  supper  generally  consisted  of  bread  and  water; 
everything  else  provided  for  him  by  the  nuns  was 
sent  to  the  sick  in  the  hospital.  He  served  those 
who  were  suffering  from  contagious  disorders 
with  even  greater  zeal ;  it  is  incredible  how 
anxious  he  was  that  they  should  want  for  nothing 
for  the  comfort  either  of  body  or  soul.    The  hos-

pital  of  S.  Lazarus  in  Valencia,  destined  for  leprous 
patients,  was  particularly  dear  to  Blessed  Nicholas, 
since  they  were  generally  shunned  on  account  of 
the  extremely  loathsome  and  infectious  nature  of 
their  malady  ;  he  devoted  himself  to  them,  washing 
them  from  head  to  foot,  refreshing  them  with 
odiferous  waters,  feeding  them,  and  cleansing  and 
making  their  beds,  he  undressed  them  and  pre- 
pared them  for  sleep,  and  then  kneeling  down,  he 
respectfully  kissed  them.  By  an  extraordinary 
impulse  of  the  Holy  Ghost,  he  sometimes  drank  a 
quantity  of  the  water  in  which  he  had  washed  the 
most  loathsome  of  the  lepers.  A  priest  who  once 
saw  him  do  this  in  the  hospital  at  Valencia,  said  to 
him,  "  Father  Nicholas,  you  are  tempting  God  by 
drinking  that  filth  ;  you  are  exposing  yourself  not 
only  to  the  leprosy,  but  to  death."  Blessed  Ni- 
cholas heaved  a  deep  sigh,and  answered:  "Ah, 
brother,  brother,  too  deeply  do  I  feel  the  leprosy 
of  my  sins,  and  this  water,  which  seems  so  disgust- 
ing to  you,  may  perhaps  wash  away  my  internal 
leprosy." 

Nor  was  his  charity  less  active  in  favour  of 
those  suffering  from  incurable  complaints ;  when- 
ever he  could  he  dressed  their  wounds  himself, 
and  provided  them  with  whatever  was  necessary 
for  them ;  he  often  licked  the  most  fetid  sores, 
and  sucked  out  all  the  putrid  matter,  after  which 
he  kissed  the  feet  of  the  poor  patients ;  when 
asked  why  he  did  so,  he  answered  that  he  kissed 
Jesus  Christ  and  His  precious  wounds  in  the  per- 
sons of  those  poor  miserable  objects.

them  to  perform  such  extraordinary  acts  of  Chris- 
tian charity  towards  the  poor ;  for  our  Lord  was 
pleased  to  confirm  and  glorify  the  charity  of  His

A  rich  friend  of  his,  a  pious  man,  gave  him 
a  quantity  of  fine  preserve,  which  he  gave  in

wards, as  he  was  celebrating  mass,  holding  the 
sacred  host  in  his  hands  after  the  consecration,  he 
distinctly  heard  our  Lord  say  these  words :  "  Why 
dost  thou  leave  Me  for  creatures  ?"  Nicholas  was 
petrified ;  yet  in  no  way  could  he  explain  to  him. 
self  the  meaning  of  these  words,  nor  could  he 
guess  what  particular  defect  it  was  for  which  our 
Lord  thus  reproached  him.  He  fasted  rigorously 
the  whole  day,  which  he  spent  in  prayer  and  tears, 
beseeching  the  Lord  to  make  known  His  will,  and

th8  fault  which  he  had  committed.  The  next

A  lady  in  Valencia  gave  a  delicious  tart  to  his

holas ate  it.  On  quitting  the  lady's  house,  he 
went  direct  to  the  hospital  of  S.  Lazarus :  after 
cleansing  the  lepers  as  usual,  they  sat  down  to 
table,  and  he  desired  his  companion  to  produce  the

whereupon  his  companion  and  the  patients  were 
unanimously  of  opinion  that  Almighty  God  had 
miraculously  multiplied  the  tart  in  his  hands.

CHAPTER  VI. 

HIS  CHARITY  FOR  THE  SPIRITUAL  WELFARE  OF  HIS 
NEIGHBOUR. 

The  salvation  and  spiritual  welfare  of  his  neigh- 
bour were  the  chief  objects  of  Blessed  Nicholas's 
heroic  charity  ;  all  his  acts  of  corporal  mercy  to 
the  poor,  the  sick,  and  every  sort  of  person,  were 
directed  by  him  to  their  sanctification.  His  alms 
and  his  services  in  the  hospitals  were  always 
accompanied  by  some  spiritual  exhortation,  or 
some  efficacious  admonition,  suited  to  the  necessi- 
ties of  each  individual.  And  he  did  this  so 
naturally  and  affably,  that  persons  of  little  or  no 
piety,  as  well  as  persons  of  high  rank,  could 
listen  to  him  with  pleasure,  and  as,  generally 
speaking,  they  stood  most  in  need  of  his  holy 
admonitions,  so  likewise  did  they  profit  most  by 
them.  His  amiable  piety  won  many,  especially 
noble  ladies,  from  a  too  worldly  and  even  scanda- 
lous life,  to  a  life  of  piety  and  edification  ;  in  this 
respect  Blessed  Nicholas  was  favoured  with  pecu- 
liar tact  and  talent. 

When  serving  the  sick  in  the  hospitals,  he 
always  touched  upon  that  point  of  spirituality 
best  suited  to  each  individual ;  he  would  read 
some  spiritual  book  when  they  were  all  assembled 
together,  and  generally  concluded  his  visit  with  a 
very  moving  sermon.    He  did  the  same  with  the

An  acquaintance  explained  two  circumstances

for  this  said  person,  earnestly  praying  that  the 
grace  of  God  might  preserve  him  from  all  evil. 

On  many  occasions  our  Lord  was  pleased  to 
glorify  his  heroic  charity  by  evident  miracles. 
He  left  his  convent  one  day,  and  on  reaching 
the  great  square  in  Valencia,  he  suddenly 
stopped,  and  said  to  his  companion,  "Let  us 
go  back and  he  ran  with  amazing  haste  to  the 
house  of  a  poor  woman,  and  anxiously  asked  to 
speak  to  her  at  the  door ;  the  woman  made  her 
appearance  in  a  state  of  great  agitation ;  he 
spoke  very  kindly  to  her  on  the  necessity  of 
Christian  patience,  and  on  the  example  given  us 
thereon  by  our  Divine  Saviour  during  His  whole 
life  on  earth,  and  more  especially  during  His 
Passion.  He  then  went  on  to  comfort  her  under 
her  own  trials,  caused  by  her  husband,  a  tyrani- 
cal  inhuman  monster ;  telling  her  that  these 
trials,  if  well  borne,  would  purchase  heaven  for 
her,  whereas  a  want  of  humble  resignation  to  the 
divine  will,  and  of  confidence  in  the  help  of  God>

would  only  redouble  her  troubles  here,  and  cause

The  holy  man  spoke  in  a  manner  which  convinced 
the  poor  woman  that  her  actual  state  of  desperation 
had  been  made  known  to  him  by  revelation.  She 
fell  down  at  his  feet  in  a  flood  of  tears,  and  owned 
publicly,  that  feeling  unable  any  longer  to  bear 
the  cruelties  of  her  husband,  she  had  fastened  a 
noose  to  one  of  the  house  beams,  and  was  actually 
up  stairs  about  to  hang  herself,  and  had  tied 
the  rope  round  her  neck,  when  a  voice  which 
must  have  proceeded  from  the  devil,  said  to  her, 
"Be  quick,  for  Father  Nicholas  is  coming ;  God 
has  revealed  thy  desperation  to  him and  at 
that  very  moment  she  was  called  down  to  the 
door.  The  saint  comforted  and  encouraged  her, 
and  reconciled  her  to  God ;  from  that  time  she 
became  a  model  of  patience  and  humble  resig- 
nation. 

Whilst  he  was  living  at  the  monastery  of  S. 
Maria  di  Gesu  at  Valencia,  he  unexpectedly  left  his 
cell  one  night,  and  hurried  towards  the  porter's 
room  ;  one  of  the  religious  tried  to  stop  him,  but 
he,  in  a  state  of  ecstasy,  bade  him  not  detain 
him ;  on  reaching  the  door,  he  bade  the  porter, 
in  a  voice  more  than  human,  to  open  the  door 
instantly;  the  brother  obeyed,  and  the  whole 
house  was  in  astonishment  at  so  unusual  a  pro- 
ceeding, especially  as  he  had  rushed  out  of  the 
house  without  going  to  receive  the  superior's 
blessing.  He,  however,  pursued  his  way,  and 
ran  on  till  he  came  to  a  field,  where  he  found  a 
man  fastening  a  rope  to  the  branch  of  a  tree,

intending  to  commit  suicide.  Nicholas  untied 
the  rope,  consoled  the  man,  and  took  him  back 
with  him  to  the  monastery,  where  he  was  kept 
for  a  few  days.  He  made  his  confession  to  Blessed 
Nicholas,  and  went  away  quite  composed  and 
happy,  and  fully  sensible  of  the  enormity  of  the 
crime  of  which  he  was  so  nearly  rendering  him- 
self guilty. 

As  he  was  once  going  to  preach  a  sermon,  on 
reaching  the  bridge  of  S.  Andrew  in  Valencia, 
he  rather  slackened  his  pace,  moved  to  a  little 
distance  from  his  companion,  and  began  to  speak 
to  a  man  who  met  them  ;  after  he  had  spoken  a  few 
words,  he  .raised  the  man's  cloak  and  drew  out 
a  dagger,  concealed  under  his  arm  ;  hereupon  the 
poor  creature  burst  into  tears,  and  fell  on  his  knees 
at  the  father's  feet ;  a  crowd  gathered  round 
them,  eager  to  know  what  was  going  on.  The 
poor  man,  in  a  fit  of  despair,  was  going  off  .  to  kill 
himself,  and  Blessed  Nicholas,  apprized  of  it  by 
revelation,  stopped  him,  as  we  have  narrated ;  he 
raised  him  from  the  ground,  comforted  him,  filled 
him  with  tender  confidence  in  the  infinite  good- 
ness of  God,  and  left  him  sincerely  penitent,  and 
determined  to  enter  upon  a  Christian  course  of 
life,  as  in  fact  he  did. 

At  the  time  our  saint  was  living  with  the 
Capuchins  in  the  monastery  called  Monte  Cal- 
vario,  beyond  the  walls  of  Barcelona,  he  sud- 
denly went  to  the  father-guardian  one  night,  and 
asked  permission  for  himself  and  a  companion  to 
go  into  the  city.  The  superior  answered  that 
they  could  not  go  out  during  the  night,  but

Blessed  Nicholas  told  him  he  had  an  order  from 
God  to  go  out  there  and  then,  on  an  affair  of  im- 
portance and  necessity.  The  guardian,  who  was 
well  acquainted  with  Nicholas's  sanctity,  appointed 
a  companion,  and  ordered  the  door  to  be  opened 
for  him.  Soon  after  he  met  a  cavalier  galloping 
along  on  a  mule.  Nicholas  sainted  him,  and  in- 
quired  where  he  was  going  at  that  hour,  and  in  such 
haste.  The  rider  answered  that  he  was  going  from 
his  country-house  to  Barcelona  on  business  of  im- 
portance, and  as  he  said  this,  he  spurred  his  mule. 
Nicholas  seized  the  bridle,  and  held  back  the 
animal  by  main  force.  The  cavalier,  in  a  pet, 
spurred  the  mule  again,  which  gave  an  impetuous 
start,  and  stepped  on  the  holy  man's  foot,  who 
nevertheless  held  the  bridle  firmly:  "Now,  Sir," 
said  he,  "  where  is  it  that  your  are  going  ?  are 
your  designs  those  of  a  Christian  cavalier  ?  And 
what  is  it  that  you  have  concealed  there  under 
your  arm?"  "I  am  astonished,"  said  the  gen- 
tleman, "that  you  speak  in  this  manner  to  such 
a  person  as  myself !  I  have  got  nothing  beneath 
my  arm."  "Yes,  yes,"  said  Blessed  Nicholas, 
with  a  smile,  "you  carry  an  evil  ornament  be- 
neath this  arm,"  and  loosening  his  coat  a  little, 
he  drew  forth  a  dagger ;  with  much  gentle  en- 
treaty be  induced  the  cavalier  to  dismount,  and 
return  with  him  to  the  monastery,  where  he 
owned  that  he  had  formed  the  desperate  resolu- 
tion of  stabbing  himself,  thus  to  put  an  end  to 
his  own  life.  He  made  his  confession,  and  in  a 
few  days  took  leave  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  full  of 
Christian  confidence  in  Divine  mercy,  and  of  sin-

Blessed  Nicholas  was  residing  at  the  monastery 
of  Escornalbou,  when  one  night  a  good  country- 
man, who  lived  at  some  distance  from  the  monas- 
tery, was  suddenly  awoke  by  a,  loud  knocking  at 
his  door,  and  by  hearing  himself  called  upon ;  he 
recognized  the  voice  as  Father  Nicholas's,  and 
hastened  to  admit  him:  "Father  Nicholas," 
said  he,  "whatever  brings  you  here  at  this 
hour,  and  on  such  a  windy  night,  too  ?"  Nicholas 
answered,  "Brother,  God  sends  me,  and  His 
angels  guide  me ;  I  am  going  to  rescue  a  despe- 
rate and  miserable  sinner  from  temporal  and  eter- 
nal death.  You  must  furnish  me  with  a  good 
courser,  and  a  sure  guide  to  go  with  me  as  far 
as  the  bridge  of  Vails.  The  worthy  farmer 
soon  saddled  a  famous  mule,  and  gave  him  a 
trusty  guide.  He  reached  the  said  bridge  by  day- 
light, and  dismounted.  A  traveller  almost  imme- 
diately crossed  the  bridge ;  Nicholas  advanced, 
raised  his  cloak,  and  drew  forth  a  dagger,  with 
which  the  wretched  man  was  actually  going  to 
commit  suicide ;  hereupon,  calling  his  guide,  he 
bade  him  return  home  with  his  mule,  as  he  in- 
tended  to  stay  with  the  poor  man ;  who,  comforted 
and  strengthened  by  the  salutary  suggestions  of 
Blessed  Nicholas,  sincerely  deplored  his  iniqui- 
ties ;  and  by  the  Divine  mercy  was  rescued  from 
a  double  death,  viz.,  of  soul  and  body.  In  the 
meantime,  a  religious  of  Escornalbou  called  at  the 
house  of  the  countryman  who  had  provided  the

CHAPTER  VII. 

HIS  HEROIC  HUMILITY. 


lit  ' 

^  It  is  known  to  all,  that  after  long,  mature,  and 

rigid  investigation,  the  Sacred  Congregation  of 
,  ^  Rites,  confirmed  by  the  Sovereign  Pontiff,  has  de- 
^  clared  that  Blessed  Nicholas  Fattore  possessed  in 
j  a  heroic  degree,  not  only  the  theological,  but  like- 
wise the  cardinal  virtues,  and  such  others  as  are 
annexed  to  them.  In  a  compendium  like  this 
it  is  impossible  to  descant  on  the  many  acts  of 
virtue  juridically  attested  in  the  processes  ;  it  will 
suffice  therefore  to  select  those  in  which  our  Lord 
was  pleased  to  distinguish  the  spirit  of  Blessed 
Nicholas  in  the  most  special  manner.  We  will 
begin  with  his  humility,  since  this  is  justly  styled 
the  foundation  of  all  christian  virtues. 

His  humble  demeanour  in  his  very  childhood 
towards  poor  mendicants,  and  later  towards  hi3 

31 


Google 


482 


NICHOLAS  FATTORE. 


novices,  is  good  evidence  of  the  degree  of  perfec- 
tion to  which  he  carried  this  virtue.  He  had  fre- 
quently on  his  lips,  and  still  more  frequently  in 
his  mind,  these  impressive  words :  "  Who  art  thou, 
O  God  !  and  who  am  I?"  Then  developing  the 
idea,  he  would  go  on  thus :  "  Thou,  0  God,  art 
what  Thou  art ;  and  I  am  dust,  ashes,  and  no- 
thingness." He  habitually  and  keenly  appre- 
hended the  greatness  of  God  as  far  as  a  creature 
having  faith  in  Jesus  Christ  can  possibly  do  so ; 
whilst  he  keenly,  habitually,  and  practically  appre- 
hended his  own  nothingness.  Suffice  it  to  say, 
Blessed  Nicholas  was  perfectly  humble  of  heart. 
No  one,  however,  can  duly  understand  and  appre- 
ciate the  above  question  and  answer,  as  applied  to 
himself  by  our  saint,  who  is  not  taught  by  divine 
wisdom ;  and  this  is  a  privilege  exclusively  re- 
served to  the  saints  of  the  Catholic  Church,  the 
perfect  possessors  of  Christian  humility,  and 
these,  in  comparison  with  the  imperfect,  will 
ever  form  a  very  small  minority. 

Descending,  however,  to  more  common  acts,  we 
may  observe  that  when  he  was  in  company  with 
the  other  religious,  either  in  the  choir,  refectory, 
chapter,  or  elsewhere,  he  felt  a  sort  of  inward 
dread,  looking  upon  himself  as  another  Judas  in 
the  midst  of  his  holy  brethren ;  he  sincerely  be- 
lieved himself  to  be  unworthy  to  wear  the  habit  of 
S.  Francis ;  and  that  he  was  the  dishonour  and 
opprobrium,  not  only  of  the  whole  order,  but  also  of 
the  whole  human  race. 

Although  he  was  considered  one  of  the  most 
learned,  as  well  as  one  of  the  most  spiritual  men

in  Spain,  and  one  of  the  most  experienced  directors 
of  the  Catholic  Church,  he  would  always  and  en- 
tirely depend  on  his  superiors,  just  as  if  he  were 
a  young  inexperienced  novice.  Every  one  who 
was  distinguished  for  sanctity  and  learning  was 
consulted  by  Blessed  Nicholas  as  to  what  pen- 
ance  he  ought  to  perform  for  his  enormous  sins, 
and  to  secure  his  salvation.  Whilst  he  was  guar- 
dian at  the  Valle  di  Gesu,  he  heard  of  a  certain  holy 
man  exceedingly  well  versed  in  a  spiritual  life, 
who  was  living  about  fifty  miles  off.  He  imme- 
diately set  off,  barefoot,  to  consult  him;  with 
much  simplicity  he  disclosed  what  he  called  his 
malice  to  him,  and  listened  to  the  words  of  the 
good  religious  as  if  they  proceeded  from  the 
mouth  of  God,  continually  thanking  the  Lord 
for  enlightening  him  by  means  of  this  His  ser- 
vant. If  he  fell  into  any  defect,  or  what  he  con- 
sidered such,  he  publicly  accused  himself  of  it, 
that  he  might  be  the  more  contemned.  Whilst  he 
was  guardian,  he  had  five  young  religious  to  pre- 
sent to  the  bishop  for  ordination;  on  the  way 
they  met  with  some  poor  people,  when  turning  to 
his  young  religious,  he  said,  "Brothers,  these 
poor  are  the  representatives  of  Jesus  Christ ;  let 
us  humble  ourselves  before  Him  by  kissing  their 
feet they  did  so,  he  setting  them  the  example. 
Being  asked  to  give  a  sermon  iu  a  town  about  a 
league's  distance  from  Valencia,  when  he  and  sev- 
eral companions  went  to  take  a  walk  after  the  ser- 
mon, they  perceived  a  cross  at  a  little  distance, 
which  he  saluted,  and  encouraged  the  rest  to  do 
the  same,  and  to  keep  silence ;  after  a  brief  inter-

val  he  resumed  the  conversation  on  spiritual  sub- 
jects ;  one  of  his  companions,  wishing  to  test  his 
virtue,  whispered  in  his  ear :  "  You  recommend 
silence  to  others,  but  do  not  observe  it  yourself; 
you  deserve  a  good  penance."  The  saint  imme- 
diately knelt  down,  and  with  great  humility  and 
contrition  acknowledged  the  fault  he  had  com- 
mitted in  breaking  silence,  asked  pardon  for  the 
scandal  he  had  given,  and  begged  that  a  suitable 
penance  might  be  imposed  upon  him ;  they  were 
all  extremely  edified,  and  had  great  difficulty  in 
persuading  him  to  rise  from  the  ground. 

The  most  Reverend  Father  Francis  di  Zamora, 
General  of  our  order,  went  to  Valencia,  and 
being  convinced  of  Blessed  Nicholas's  merits  and 
of  his  aptitude  of  pen,  selected  him  for  his  secre- 
tary, a  post  of  high  importance.  Nicholas  was 
extremely  distressed  at  this  honourable  appoint- 
ment, he  so  exaggerated  his  incompetency  and 
demerits,  and  wept  so  bitterly,  that  the  Father 
General,  surprised  and  edified  by  his  wonderful 
humility,  (unwilling  to  afflict  him  too  much) 
accepted  his  excuses,  consoled  him,  and  bade  him 
continually  pray  to  God  for  himself  and  for  the 
whole  order. 

When  not  otherwise  occupied,  he  used  to  go  to 
the  kitchen,  and  ask  the  cook  to  employ  him  in 
the  vilest  offices ;  if  the  cook,  out  of  respect, 
begged  him  to  withdraw  from  the  kitchen,  a 
place  so  unsuited  for  one  of  his  worth,  he  would 
throw  himself  upon  his  kuees,  and  weeping,  en- 
treat him  not  to  speak  in  such  a  style,  assuring 
him  that  he  was  mistaken,  for  that  he  was  a  hypo-

crite,  a  great  sinner,  and  so  at  last  he  gained  his 
point.  To  prevent  him  from  humbling  himself 
still  more,  the  cooks  would  employ  him  in  wash- 
ing the  stew-pans,  sweeping,  or  carrying  wood. 

As  he  was  once  walking  barefoot  and  bare- 
headed towards  the  city  of  Segorbe,  he  met  a 
gentleman  on  horseback,  who  was  well  acquainted 
with  the  Father  and  his  exalted  virtue.  See- 
ing him  with  his  companion,  bathed  in  perspira- 
tion and  covered  with  dust,  he  dismounted,  and 
earnestly  entreated  him  for  the  love  of  God  to 
mount  his  horse,  and  so  spare  himself  a  little  of 
the  fatigue  to  which  he  exposed  himself ;  adding, 
that  it  was  too  bad  of  him  to  hazard  a  life  on 
which  the  spiritual  welfare  of  so  many  people  in 
Spain  depended.  Blessed  Nicholas  was  horrified 
at  these  words ;  he  threw  himself  flat  upon  his  back 
on  the  ground,  beseeching  the  gentleman  and  hig 
companion  to  beat  him  on  the  mouth,  because  he 
was  the  greatest  sinner  in  the  world  ;  the  gentle- 
man who  was  much  edified  by  his  humility,  was 
obliged  to  let  him  pursue  his  journey  bare-footed 
and  bare-headed,  as  the  only  means  of  inducing 
him  to  rise. 

A  person  who  had  a  great  regard  for  him 
happened  one  day  to  allude  to  something  done  by 
Nicholas,  to  the  advantage  and  edification  of 
many ;  seeing  that  his  remarks  were  displeasing 
to  the  holy  man,  cautious  and  moderate  as  they 
were,  he  adroitly  changed  his  style,  adding,  that 
God  alone  is  the  author  of  all  good,  and  that  to 
Him  alone  was  due  the  edification  and  spiritual 
profit  effected  by  Father  Fattore,  that  God  often

promotes  the  good  of  others  by  means  of  the 
wicked,  and  that  Father  Fattpre  might  be  one  of 
this  stamp;  indeed,  he  strongly  suspected, that 
instead  of  being  a  saint,  he  was,  in  fact,  a  hypocrite 
and  impostor,  but  that  the  Lord  knows  how  to 
turn  the  mistakes  and  scandals  of  sinners  into

he  concluded  by  saying  that  he  wished  Father 
Nicholas  every  good,  but,  to  tell  him  sincerely  his 
opinion  of  him,  it  was  that  he  was  just  good  for 
nothing,  and  unworthy  of  the  bread  he  ate.  The 
holy  man  showed  himself  highly  pleased  with 
these  remarks,  and  was  more  cordial  than  ever 
with  his  worthy  friend ;  he  must  have  been  a  man 
of  great  good  sense,  who  could  with  such  innocent 
tact  cheat  so  great  a  saint.  It  seems  that 
Almighty  God  would  on  this  occasion  glorify  the 
humility  of  Blessed  Nicholas,  and  the  innocent 
fraud  of  his  friend,  since  during  the  conversation, 
which  must  have  been  pretty  long,  the  joy  of  the 
former  threw  him  into  an  ecstasy. 

Some  of  the  religious,  who  acted  as  his  com- 
panions, would  often  for  their  own  edification  and 
instruction,  dexterously  watch  his  words  and  ac- 
tions, on  purpose  to  be  able  to  reprove  him; 
the  reprehensions  were  feigned,  it  is  true,  but 
were  often  sufficiently  caustic  ;  nevertheless,  they 
were  always  gratefully  acknowledged,  and  the' 
faults  humbly  confessed,  with  the  usual  admission 
that  he  was  indeed  a  great  sinner,  who  did 
nothing  without  falling  into  some  considerable 
fault.

CHAPTER  VIII. 

HIS  HEROIC  MORTIFICATION. 

Whoever  knows,  by  divine  light,  his  own 
nothingness,  and  the  misery  and  malice  of  human 
nature,  depraved  by  original  sin,  cannot  do  other- 
wise than  have  a  holy  hatred  of  self,  or  fail  to 
contradict  the  natural  inclinations,  which  either 
are  vicious,  or  may  become  so,  unless  contin- 
ually curbed  by  the  mortification  of  Jesus  Christ. 
As  in  other  virtues,  so  likewise  was  Blessed 
Nicholas  perfect  in  this ;  if  we  wished  to  pick  out 
of  the  processes  some  difficulty  on  the  point  of  his 
virtues,  we  think  it  would  be  in  the  excess,  not  in 
any  defect  of  his  mortification,  only  that  we  know 
on  the  other  hand,  that  in  no  particular  act  did 
he  ever  yield  to  excess,  though  at  first  sight  it 
might  appear  as  if  he  had  done  so ;  he  was  moved 
by  a  special  impulse  of  the  Most  High,  whose 
omnipotence  has  no  limits.  For  fourteen  years 
he  went  bare-foot,  winter  and  summer ;  in  his 
latter  years,  by  the  advice  of  the  doctors,  his 
superiors  obliged  him  to  wear  sandals*  His 
usual  bed  was  a  bundle  of  vines,  with  a  log  of 
wood  or  a  stone  for  his  pillow ;  if  by  chance  he 
lay  down  on  a  bench  or  a  board,  he  used  to  think 
himself  too  luxuriously  lodged.  He  rose  every 
night  to  matins,  after  which  he  allowed  himself  no 
more  sleep,  remaining  in  the  choir,  generally  with 
his  arms  outstretched  in  the  form  of  a  cross,  contem-

plating  with  abundance  of  tender  tears,  his  dear 
Saviour  agonizing  on  a  cross  for  love  of  us.  He  dis- 
ciplined himself  for  some  hours  every  night ;  his 
discipline  was  not  only  heavy,  but  was  moreover 
furnished  with  sharp  iron  rowels.  He  used  in 
disciplining  himself  to  strike  from  head  to  foot, 
saying,  «■  It  is  written  of  our  Lord, '  From  the  sole 
of  the  foot  to  the  top  of  the  head  there  is  no

only  his  upper  tunic,  under  which  his  whole 
person  was  enveloped  in  very  rough  hair-cloth; 
besides  his  hair-shirt,  he  had  another  still  more 
painful,  which  he  reserved  for  the  vigils  of  the 
principal  festivals,  or  other  occasions  of  private 
devotion,  especially  when  he  had  any  very  particu- 
lar prayer  to  offer.  His  continual  disciplines 
and  his  hair-shirt  reduced  his  body  to  one  large 
wound ;  there  was  one  religious  whom  he  made 
his  confidant,  and  whom  he  used  to  ask  to  dress 
his  wounds,  when  absolutely  necessary,  taking 
care  always  to  bind  him  down  to"  strict  secrecy. 
Salt  and  vinegar  was  the  only  remedy  he  would 
ever  admit  of. 

Often  in  the  morning,  in  the  very  depth  of 
winter,  he  would  retire  to  the  convent  garden, 
where,  undressing  himself,  he  would  remain 
exposed  to  the  cold,  or  perhaps  plunge  into  a 
stagnant  frozen  pond,  and  there  stay  for  a  consi- 
derable time.  His  fasting  might  almost  be 
called  daily,  so  sparing  was  he  in  his  diet,  and 
this  even  at  the  table  of  distinguished  persons, 
who  often  wished  to  have  him  for  their  guest. 
In  Lent,  he  seldom  took  anything  but  bread  and

One  evening,  a  judge  of  the  royal  audience-

flying  in  so  much  haste  ?"  Nicholas,  half  smiling 
and  half  frowning,  answered:  "Flying?  yes,  I 
am  flying  from  the  city  of  Segorbe,  and  with 
good  reason;  the  people  there  in  cruel  charity 
strove  to  render  me  an  enemy  to  the  cross  of  Jesus 
Christ,  and  I,  to  avoid  this  irreparable  misfortune, 
am  flying  away/' 

Once,  in  a  tolerably  severe  winter,  as  he  was 
going  from  Valencia  to  Albayda,  to  preach,  he

of  this,  and  facts  convinced  superiors  that  God 
required  these  extraordinary  rigours  of  him ;  that 
they  in  no  degree  prejudiced  his  health,  and  being 
convinced  of  this,  they  consented  to  them. 


CHAPTER  IX. 

TRIALS  OCCASIONED  BY  THE  DEVIL. 

Almighty  God,  who  by  means  of  heroic  morti- 
fication, a  mortification  far  beyond  the  ordinary 
powers  of  human  nature,  would  have  Blessed 
Nicholas  conformed  to  the  image  of  His  Divine 
Son  crucified  for  love  of  us ;  would,  in  addition 
to  his  habitual  rigours,  permit  the  devil  to  afflict 
and  torment  him  in  several  ways,  and  for  a  consi- 
derable time.

One  night,  as  a  worthy  religious  remained  in 
the  choir  after  matins  to  pray,  Blessed  Nicholas, 
who,  as  usual,  did  not  return  to  his  cell,  retired 
to  a  side  chapel  to  continue  his  devotions ;  all 
the  others  were  gone,  and  profound  silence  reigned 
throughout  the  church,  when,  all  at  ouce,  the 
religious  who  was  in  the  choir,  heard  a-  great 
noise  as  of  persons  struggling  violently.  The 
contest  was  long,  and  sometimes  noisy ;  at  last, 
he  heard  Blessed  Nicholas  exclaim,  in  an  anxious 
tone,  "Vile  houud,  dost  thou  think  to  strangle 
me  ?  I  do  not  fear  thee  at  all  I  My  Sa-

thyself,  since  the  vices  of  my  flesh  are  the  best 
weapons  which  thou  couldst  use  against  my 
soul!" 

Another  night,  as  he  was  praying  in  the  same 
church  after  matins,  the  devil  in  most  frightful 
form  appeared  to  him,  seized  him  by  the  throat, 
tried  to  strangle  him,  and  beat  him  unmercifully 
for  a  long  time,  so  as  almost  to  kill  him ;  after 
suffering  thus  grievously,  our  Divine  Saviour  ap- 
peared, when  the  prince  of  darkness  immediately 
vanished.  Our  Lord  said  a  few  words  to  him 
witli  much  affection,  and  they  sufficed  to  fill  his 
soul  with  ineffable  delight,  and  to  comfort  and 
invigorate  his  whole  person. 

Another  night,  in  the  church  of  the  Valle  di 
Gesu,  as  he  was  in  prayer  before  matins,  two 
frightful  Moors  made  their  appearance;  they 
were  of  such  gigantic  stature  as  to  touch  the  roof

Whilst  he  was  confessor  to  the  nuns,  he  used

more  anxious  lest  some  offence  should  be  com- 
mitted, than  at  the  assaults  directed  against  him- 
self. But  generally  speaking,  his  anguish  on  this 
score  was  relieved  by  our  Lord,  who  gave  him

One  night  as  he  was  praying  in  the  church  for

"In  my  youth,"  said  he,  "the  devils  tormented

the  good  religious  was  free  from  the  temptations 
of  the  devil. 


CHAPTER  X. 

OBSERVANCE  OF  HIS  RELIGIOUS  VOWS. 

The  perfect  observance  of  poverty,  chastity, 
and  obedience,  which  all  religious  bind  them- 
selves to  by  vow  at  their  solemn  profession,  sub- 
stantially constitutes  their  sanctity ;  and  the  more 


Digitized  by  Google 


496 


NICHOLAS  PATTOBE. 


perfectly  they  observe  these  three  vows,  according 
to  the  constitutions  of  their  respective  institutes 
approved  by  the  Church,  the  greater  will  be 
their  perfection,  and  the  more  holy  and  pleasing 
'  will  they  be  in  the  sight  of  God. 

Blessed  Nicholas  was  so  exact  and  perfect  in 
the  observance  of  obedience,  that  it  was  sufficient 
to  say  that  the  Church,  or  the  Franciscan  rules, 
or  a  superior,  wanted  anything,  for  him  to  exe- 
cute it  willingly  and  promptly.  Throughout  his 
religious  career,  even  in  the  most  trivial  things, 
he  would  always  depend  on  obedience,  aud  ask 
leave  of  proper  superiors.  In  his  journeys,  his 
companion,  though  perhaps  only  a  novice  or  a 
lay-brother,  was  always  constituted  by  him  to 
act  as  his  superior ;  he  halted,  or  went  on,  just 
as  his  companion  pleased,  so  that  any  one  who 
accompanied  him  knew  very  well  that  he  must 
act  the  master.  Much  as  he  was  addicted  to 
mortification,  he  immediately  desisted  from  any 
specific  act  of  it,  and  from  any  sort  of  penance  if 
he  knew  his  superior  disapproved  of  it.  Docile 
as  he  was,  both  by  nature  and  by  virtue,  it  is 
true  to  say  that  superiors  did  not  deem  it  advisa- 
ble to  restrain  him,  either  in  his  personal  austeri- 
ties, or  in  his  extraordinary  proceedings  in  the 
hospitals,  as  already  related ;  because  they  were 
convinced  Almighty  God  required  these  unusual 
practices  on  his  part,  which  would  certainly  not 
have  been  permitted  on  any  other  grounds. 

Nor  was  he  less  exact  on  the  score  of  holy 
poverty,  which,  as  every  one  knows,  is  most 
strict  and  rigorous  in  the  Franciscan  order.  He

497 


never  had  more  than  one  tunic  and  a  cloak, 
which,  generally  speaking,  had  been  worn  by 
others,  and  was  mended,  but  clean.  In  his  room 
he  had  nothing  but  what  was  strictly  necessary, 
and  his  things  were  always  the  oldest  in  the 
house.  He  had  but  two  books,  the  holy  scrip- 
tures and  his  breviary ;  if  he  had  occasion  for  any 
others  for  the  composition  of  his  sermons,  he  re- 
turned them  as  soon  as  finished  with,  or  if  they 
were  given  to  him,  he  asked  leave  to  dispose  of 
them  to  some  one  else,  he  did  the  same  with  what- 
ever he  received  from  his  friends  and  penitents,  and 
he  had  many :  all  was  in  one  way  or  other  made 
over  to  the  poor.  To  sum  up  all  in  one  word,  it 
seems  to  me  that  if  the  seraphical  patriarch  S. 
Francis  was  one  of  the  most  perfect  observers  of 
poverty  ever  witnessed  in  the  church  of  God, 
so  Blessed  Nicholas  Fattore  was  one  of  the  sons  of 
S.  Francis,  who  most  resembled  him  in  this  virtue. 
He  had  a  great  respect  for  pious  pictures,  yet  he 
would  never  gratify  his  own  devotion  so  far  as  to 
keep  even  one  in  his  room,  if  it  was  of  the  least 
value. 

His  chastity  in  its  substantial  perfection,  was 
like  the  purity  of  the  angels,  though  unlike  theirs 
in  being  subject  to  temptation.  As  man,  he  was 
composed  of  two  discordant  parts;  and  as  such 
he  had  to  undergo  the  conflict  natural  to  man. 
We  have  seen  in  the  first  book  his  dangerous 
temptation,  and  his  glorious  victory  on  this  sub- 
ject; this  event  occurred  when  he  was  in  the 
full  prime  of  life.  We  may  here  add  two  other 
instances  equally  edifying  and  honourable.

NICHOLAS  FATTOKE. 


Whilst  he  was  the  Guardian  of  the  monastery 
of  Valle  di  Gesu,  being  then  but  young,  he  was 
one  day  assailed  in  a  most  trying  manner, 
experiencing  that  baneful  law  of  the  members, 
which  revolts  against  the  law  of  the  mind,  and 
the  law  of  the  body,  which  strove  to  make  him 
the  slave  of  sin.  In  terror  he  humbled  himself, 
weeping  and  calling  on  the  Lord.  The  struggle, 
however,  augmented  ;  impelled  by  a  superior  im- 
pulse he  arose,  and  though  it  was  in  the  depth 
of  winter,  he  ran  towards  a  pond  covered  over 
with  ice,  and  tearing  off  his  clothes,  plunged  in 
up  to  the  neck,  and  there  remained  petrified 
with  cold,  till  the  rebellion  of  his  corrupt  na- 
ture bad  totally  subdued.  Although  icicles  dung 
to  his  person,  he  had  rendered  the  water  abso- 
lutely hot  and  boiling.  With  bare  shoulders 
Blessed  Nicholas  carried  a  large  cross  on  his 
back,  and  in  this  state  entered  the  refectory, 
where  all  the  religious  were  at  table ;  he  knelt 
down  in  the  middle  of  the  room,  and  with  tears  of 
deep  contrition  he  declared  that  he  was  the  great- 
est of  sinners,  guilty  of  innumerable  crimes  and 
dreadful  scandals ;  beseeching  the  fathers  in 
charity  to  impose  some  penance  on  him.  The 
Father-Vicar  bade  him  kiss  the  feet  of  the  religious, 
and  then  go  and  dress  himself.  Instead  of  ris- 
ing on  his  feet>  he  crawled  on  his  knees  round  the 
refectory,  kissed  the  feet  of  all,  with  a  lively  feel- 
ing of  humble  sorrow,  and  then  crawled  out  of  the 
room.  In  the  house  of  S.  Maria  di  Gesu,  on  the 
eve  of  the  festival  of  S.  Ursula,  he  was  preparing 
a  sermon  which  he  was  to  deliver  the  next  day,  in

moreover,  favoured  him  so  sensibly,  that  on  enter- 
ing the  convents  of  virgins  consecrated  to  God,  he 
smelt  a  particular  fragrance,  and  experienced  an 
indescribable  delight ;  in  his  excess  of  joy,  he
